topics.name: Life and importance of the Prophet (pbuh)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events of the first revelation to the Prophet (pbuh) and what happened immediately afterwards.
parts.answer: At about the age of 40 (610 CE) the Prophet (pbuh) was meditating in the cave of Hira when the angel Jibril came and told him to read; he said he could not read; the angel pressed him three times and then revealed the first verses of Sura 96 (Iqra); he returned home shaken and asked Khadija to cover him; she comforted him, reminding him of his good character, and took him to her cousin Waraqa bin Naufal, who said this was the same angel who had come to Moses and warned that his people would drive him out.
parts.working: Indicative content: Age about 40 / month of Ramadan; retreat in the cave of Hira on Mount Nur; Jibril appeared and commanded 'Read'; the Prophet (pbuh) replied that he could not read; the angel embraced / squeezed him three times; the first verses of Sura 96.1–5 were revealed; he returned trembling and asked to be wrapped up; Khadija reassured him (he is kind to relatives, helps the weak, honours guests); visit to Waraqa bin Naufal; Waraqa confirmed it was the angel who came to Moses and predicted opposition. parts.label: b
parts.text: What can Muslim husbands and wives learn from Khadija's response? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Spouses should support each other in hard times, listen calmly, encourage each other's good qualities and seek wise advice together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the persecution suffered by early Muslims in Makka. Refer to named individuals.
parts.answer: Bilal was tortured by his master Umayya bin Khalaf, laid on hot sand with a rock on his chest, yet kept saying God is One, until Abu Bakr bought and freed him; Yasir and his wife Sumayya were tortured and Sumayya was killed by Abu Jahl, the first martyr of Islam; their son 'Ammar was also tortured; Khabbab bin al-Aratt was made to lie on burning coals; the Prophet (pbuh) himself was insulted, had filth thrown on him while praying and thorns placed in his path.
parts.working: Indicative content: Bilal — tortured by Umayya bin Khalaf on hot sand with a stone on his chest; repeated 'Ahad, Ahad'; freed by Abu Bakr; Sumayya — killed by Abu Jahl, the first martyr; Yasir also died under torture; 'Ammar tortured; Khabbab — burned on coals; slaves and poor Muslims suffered most; the Prophet (pbuh) was mocked and had dirt / entrails thrown on him; Abu Lahab's wife put thorns in his path. parts.text: Why do you think these early Muslims remained firm in their faith?
parts.answer: Because their faith in God and the Hereafter was stronger than fear of pain, and they were inspired by the Prophet's (pbuh) example and the promise of reward.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events of the Night Journey and Ascension (al-Isra' wal-Mi'raj).
parts.answer: One night in Makka, before the Hijra, the angel Jibril took the Prophet (pbuh) from the Sacred Mosque in Makka to al-Aqsa in Jerusalem on al-Buraq; there he led the earlier prophets in prayer; he then ascended through the heavens, meeting prophets such as Adam, Jesus, Moses and Abraham, and reached the Lote Tree of the Furthest Boundary; the five daily prayers were made obligatory (first fifty, reduced to five); in the morning the Quraysh mocked the account, but Abu Bakr believed it at once and was called al-Siddiq.
parts.working: Indicative content: Journey by night from Masjid al-Haram to Masjid al-Aqsa (mentioned in Sura 17.1); accompanied by Jibril; riding al-Buraq; led the prophets in prayer at al-Aqsa; ascension through the seven heavens; met earlier prophets (any named correctly); reached Sidrat al-Muntaha; gift of salat — fifty reduced to five on Moses's advice; Quraysh mocked / asked him to describe Jerusalem; Abu Bakr's immediate belief earned the title al-Siddiq. parts.answer: Prayer was given directly in the heavens, showing its high status; it is a daily meeting with God that keeps the believer close to Him and disciplined.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the first three years of the Prophet's (pbuh) preaching, when he invited people to Islam privately. Name the first people who accepted his message.
parts.answer: Preaching was private for about three years; the first believers were Khadija, 'Ali, Zayd ibn Haritha and Abu Bakr; Abu Bakr brought others such as 'Uthman, al-Zubayr, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Talha; believers met quietly, including at the house of al-Arqam.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): after the first revelation (610 CE) the Prophet (pbuh) first told those closest to him; Khadija was the first to believe; 'Ali, a boy in his household, accepted; Zayd ibn Haritha, his freed slave and adopted son; Abu Bakr, his close friend, a respected merchant; Abu Bakr used his influence to bring 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Talha ibn 'Ubaydullah; early converts included poor people and slaves such as Bilal; they prayed in secret, sometimes in the valleys outside Makka; the house of al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam became a meeting and teaching place; the number of believers grew slowly (a few dozen); the period ended when God commanded open preaching to his relatives. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why do you think the Prophet (pbuh) began by preaching privately rather than publicly? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: To protect the small group of believers, build a strong, well-taught core first and avoid early violent opposition before the community was ready.
parts.working: Points may include: the believers were few and weak; Makkan leaders were powerful and could crush the message early; time was needed to teach the basics of belief and prayer; a firm core group could later spread the message; it shows wisdom and planning alongside trust in God; Muslims today can learn to plan carefully before starting a big task. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happened when the Prophet (pbuh) first called people openly from Mount Safa and when he invited his relatives to a meal.
parts.answer: He called the clans of Quraysh from Safa, asked if they would believe him if he warned of an army, they said yes as he was truthful, he warned them of punishment; Abu Lahab cursed him; at the meal for Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib he invited them to Islam and only young 'Ali responded.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: God commanded him to warn his nearest relatives; he climbed Safa and called the clans; he asked whether they would believe him if he said an army was behind the hill; they replied that they had only known him to be truthful; he warned them of a severe punishment unless they believed; Abu Lahab insulted him and the gathering broke up; he invited the clan of 'Abd al-Muttalib to a meal and called them to Islam; only 'Ali, a boy, offered his support.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Prophet (pbuh) first asked the people whether they trusted him before giving his message. Explain why this was a wise way to begin.
parts.answer: It reminded them of his proven honesty (al-Amin), so they could not easily reject his message as a lie; his reputation became evidence for his message.
parts.working: Points may include: he was known as al-Sadiq and al-Amin; their own reply showed he had never lied; it made rejecting him unreasonable; it shows good character prepares people to listen; a preacher's actions must match their words; teachers and parents today gain trust before giving advice. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Prophet (pbuh) began to preach Islam openly in Makka.
parts.answer: After about three years of private preaching, God commanded him to warn his nearest relatives; he invited the Banu Hashim to a meal and called them to Islam, and only 'Ali responded; he climbed Mount Safa and called the clans of Quraysh, asking if they would believe him if he warned of an army behind the hill; they said yes as he had always been truthful; he then warned them of a severe punishment; Abu Lahab cursed him and Sura 111 was revealed about Abu Lahab.
parts.working: Indicative content: Private / secret preaching for about three years; command to warn his close relatives; invitation of the Banu Hashim to a meal; few responded, 'Ali offered support; call from Mount Safa to the Quraysh; question about an army behind the hill; people agreed he was truthful (al-Amin); warning about punishment / need to worship one God; Abu Lahab's angry reply; revelation of Sura 111; public preaching then began at the Ka'ba and to pilgrims. parts.text: Write about the ways in which the leaders of the Quraysh tried to stop the Prophet (pbuh) from preaching.
parts.answer: They mocked and called him a poet, sorcerer or madman; they pressured his uncle Abu Talib to withdraw protection; they offered him wealth, leadership or kingship through 'Utba bin Rabi'a if he stopped; they tortured weak Muslims; they tried to stop people listening to him; they imposed a social and economic boycott on the Banu Hashim; finally they plotted to kill him.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give an account of the migrations of Muslims to Abyssinia.
parts.answer: In the fifth year of prophethood (about 615 CE), because of persecution, the Prophet (pbuh) allowed a small group, including 'Uthman and his wife Ruqayya, to go to Abyssinia, ruled by a just Christian king, the Negus; a larger group followed under Ja'far bin Abi Talib; the Quraysh sent 'Amr bin al-'As and 'Abdullah bin Abi Rabi'a with gifts to have them returned; the Negus called the Muslims; Ja'far explained Islam and recited from Sura Maryam; the Negus was moved, refused to hand them over and allowed them to live in safety.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give an account of the Prophet's (pbuh) visit to Ta'if.
parts.answer: After the Year of Sorrow he went to Ta'if with Zayd bin Haritha to invite the Thaqif tribe to Islam; its leaders rejected him rudely and set street boys and slaves on him, who threw stones until he was bleeding; he sheltered in a garden and prayed to God, complaining of his weakness but seeking only God's pleasure; Addas, a Christian servant, brought him grapes and accepted his message; Jibril came with the angel of the mountains, offering to crush the people between two mountains, but he refused, hoping their descendants would worship God.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the hostility that the Prophet (pbuh) personally faced from named individuals in Makka.
parts.answer: Abu Lahab and his wife Umm Jamil insulted and harmed him; Abu Jahl abused him and plotted against him; 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt threw animal entrails on him while he prostrated and tried to strangle him; Umayya ibn Khalaf mocked him; he was called a poet, sorcerer and madman.

parts.answer: To stay patient and dignified, not reply with abuse, keep explaining the truth politely and leave the matter to God.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give an account of how Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab accepted Islam.
parts.answer: Hamza, hearing that Abu Jahl had insulted the Prophet (pbuh), struck Abu Jahl and declared his Islam; 'Umar set out to kill the Prophet, was told his sister and her husband had become Muslims, found them reading part of the Qur'an (Sura Ta-Ha), was moved, and went to the Prophet at al-Arqam's house to accept Islam.

parts.answer: Both were strong and respected, so Muslims gained confidence and protection, began to pray openly at the Ka'ba, and the Quraysh became more worried.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the boycott of the Banu Hashim and the 'Year of Sorrow'.
parts.answer: The Quraysh agreed a written boycott hung in the Ka'ba: no trade, marriage or social contact with the Banu Hashim (and Banu Muttalib) unless they handed over the Prophet (pbuh); the clan was confined to the valley of Abu Talib for about three years, suffering hunger; some sympathetic Makkans secretly sent food and later campaigned to end it; the boycott ended about the tenth year of prophethood; soon after, Abu Talib and Khadija died, so that year was called the Year of Sorrow; the Prophet (pbuh) lost his protector and his supporting wife, and persecution increased.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the reasons why the leaders of Makka opposed the message of the Prophet (pbuh).
parts.answer: Religious: it attacked the idols of their ancestors; economic: Makka earned from pilgrims visiting the idols at the Ka'ba; social: Islam made rich and poor, masters and slaves equal; political: they feared losing leadership to the Banu Hashim; belief: they rejected resurrection and accountability, which would limit their way of life.

parts.answer: They offered wealth, leadership or kingship and medical help through 'Utba ibn Rabi'a; they proposed alternating worship of God and their gods; they pressed Abu Talib; the Prophet (pbuh) refused all offers, recited the Qur'an to 'Utba, and said he would not abandon his mission even if given the sun and moon; Sura 109 rejected compromise in worship.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the change of the qibla (direction of prayer) in Madina.
parts.answer: In the second year after the Hijra, about sixteen to seventeen months after arriving, the Prophet (pbuh) was commanded to turn from Jerusalem to the Ka'ba in Makka; he turned during a prayer; the mosque where this happened is known as the mosque of the two qiblas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the hypocrites (munafiqun) in Madina and the problems they caused the Prophet (pbuh).
parts.answer: Led by 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, they claimed to be Muslim but worked against the community: withdrew about a third of the army before Uhud, spread rumours, stirred division between Emigrants and Helpers, made excuses to avoid Tabuk and built a mosque to cause harm; the Prophet (pbuh) dealt with them patiently.

parts.answer: At Badr he accepted al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir's advice on where to camp; before Uhud he agreed with the majority to go out of the city; at the Trench he accepted Salman's idea of digging a ditch; he consulted about the captives of Badr.

parts.text: Describe how the Prophet (pbuh) brought unity to Yathrib, a town divided between the Aws and the Khazraj and with Jewish and pagan clans, in his first years there.
parts.answer: He ended the Aws–Khazraj feud by uniting them as Ansar in faith, paired Emigrants and Helpers in brotherhood, built the mosque as a centre, set up the Constitution defining rights of all groups and himself as final judge, renamed the city Madina and set up a fair market.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): the Aws and Khazraj had fought for years, ending in the battle of Bu'ath; both groups accepted him as leader and arbiter; their new shared identity as Ansar replaced tribal rivalry; the mu'akhat paired each Emigrant with a Helper; the mosque was built with everyone taking part, the Prophet (pbuh) carrying bricks himself; the Charter of Madina made Muslims one community (umma) and gave the Jewish tribes freedom of religion and a duty of joint defence; disputes were to be referred to the Prophet (pbuh); a new market was set up with honest trading rules; Yathrib became 'the city of the Prophet'; he consulted people and treated all fairly. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Pakistan has many ethnic and language groups. Which of the Prophet's (pbuh) methods do you think would most help national unity today? Give reasons.
parts.answer: Any one method well argued, e.g. a written agreement of equal rights and duties (like the Charter), or brotherhood linking people across groups.
parts.working: Points may include: a written constitution guaranteeing equal rights and protection of minorities; brotherhood schemes such as student exchanges between provinces; fair institutions and markets; a shared identity above tribe and language; leaders taking part in work alongside people; reasons and a relevant example needed for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Madina period: community, treaties and diplomacy

parts.label: a
parts.text: After Hudaybiyya, a Makkan Muslim called Abu Basir escaped to Madina. Write about what happened to Abu Basir and Abu Jandal, and how the Quraysh later asked for one of the treaty's terms to be dropped.
parts.answer: Under the treaty the Prophet (pbuh) returned Abu Jandal and later Abu Basir; Abu Basir escaped his guards, settled at the coast and was joined by other Makkan Muslims; they attacked Quraysh caravans, so the Quraysh themselves asked the Prophet (pbuh) to take these men into Madina, ending that clause.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): Abu Jandal, son of the Quraysh negotiator Suhayl ibn 'Amr, arrived in chains as the treaty was being written; the Prophet (pbuh) honoured the agreement and sent him back, telling him to be patient; Muslims were distressed; later Abu Basir fled to Madina; the Quraysh sent two men to bring him back and the Prophet (pbuh) handed him over; on the way he killed one guard and escaped; the Prophet (pbuh) did not keep him in Madina; Abu Basir settled at a place on the Red Sea coast on the Quraysh trade route; Abu Jandal and other escaped Muslims joined him; they attacked Quraysh caravans; the Quraysh wrote asking the Prophet (pbuh) to accept these men into Madina and gave up the clause; the believers saw the wisdom of the treaty. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Keeping a hard promise is better than breaking it for a quick gain.' Evaluate this statement using these events.
parts.answer: The Prophet's (pbuh) patience in keeping the clause brought a better result — the clause collapsed through the Quraysh's own request — and kept Muslim credibility.
parts.working: Points may include: breaking it would have given the Quraysh a reason to cancel the peace; keeping it showed honesty; the problem was solved without Muslims breaking their word; trust is valuable in personal and international relations; but promises that require sin are not binding; balanced judgement for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Madina period: community, treaties and diplomacy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Prophet's (pbuh) relations with the three main Jewish tribes of Madina (Banu Qaynuqa', Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayza), from the Charter of Madina to the end of the Battle of the Trench.
parts.answer: The Charter gave them religious freedom and joint defence duties; Banu Qaynuqa' were exiled after a dispute in the market following Badr; Banu al-Nadir were exiled after a plot against the Prophet's (pbuh) life; Banu Qurayza sided with the enemy during the Trench and were judged by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh after it.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): the Charter recognised the Jewish tribes as part of the community with their own religion and a duty to defend Madina jointly; Banu Qaynuqa', traders and goldsmiths, broke the agreement after a quarrel in their market after Badr (2 AH), were besieged and were made to leave Madina; Banu al-Nadir plotted to drop a stone on the Prophet (pbuh) when he visited them, and in 4 AH were besieged and left for Khaybar; some of their leaders helped gather the confederate army against Madina; Banu Qurayza broke their pact during the Battle of the Trench (5 AH) by siding with the attackers; afterwards they agreed to the judgement of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, their former ally; a balanced answer notes that the Charter was a genuine agreement and the conflicts came from broken pacts in wartime, not from their religion. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What does the Charter of Madina, and the way breaches of it were treated, teach about loyalty and security in a state with people of different faiths? Explain.
parts.answer: A state can grant all groups freedom of religion and protection, but all citizens must be loyal in its defence; treaties bind both sides and their breach in wartime has serious consequences.
parts.working: Points may include: freedom of religion was guaranteed; equal duty of defence; treaties are binding on both sides; treason in war threatens everyone; individual cases were judged, not whole religions; today minorities and majorities have both rights and duties under a constitution. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give an account of the Battle of Badr.
parts.answer: In Ramadan 2 AH (624 CE) about 313 Muslims set out to intercept a Quraysh caravan led by Abu Sufyan; the caravan escaped and a Makkan army of about 1,000 marched out; the Muslims camped by the wells of Badr on advice from a Companion; the Prophet (pbuh) prayed earnestly through the night; the battle began with single combats in which Hamza, 'Ali and 'Ubayda fought; God sent angels to help and rain to firm the ground; the Muslims won; about 70 Makkans, including Abu Jahl, were killed and about 70 captured; 14 Muslims were martyred.
parts.working: Indicative content: Date (17 Ramadan 2 AH / 624); about 313 Muslims with few horses and camels; Quraysh about 1,000; cause — Abu Sufyan's caravan and Quraysh protection of it; camp near the wells (advice of al-Hubab); the Prophet's (pbuh) prayer for victory; duels — Hamza, 'Ali, 'Ubayda; help of angels / rain; Abu Jahl killed; about 70 Quraysh killed and 70 captured; 14 Muslims martyred; prisoners treated kindly, some freed for teaching ten children to read. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why do you think the victory at Badr was so important for the early Muslim community?
parts.answer: It strengthened the Muslims' faith that God supports believers, gave them status in Arabia and weakened the Quraysh leadership.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Reason, development (e.g. a small, poorly armed group defeated a large army, confirming trust in God). Model answer: It strengthened the Muslims' faith that God supports believers, gave them status in Arabia and weakened the Quraysh leadership. Marked by levels out of 4. Level 4 (4): a well-developed, reasoned answer (two developed points, or one fully developed point) linked to life today, with a clear judgement where the question asks for one. Level 3 (3): a reasoned answer with some development and a relevant example, but the judgement or link to today is less clear. Level 2 (2): one or two simple points with little development. Level 1 (1): a basic, general statement. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give an account of the expedition to Khaybar.
parts.answer: In 7 AH the Prophet (pbuh) led about 1,600 men to Khaybar, a group of fortified oases north of Madina that had become a base for enemies; the forts were taken one by one; 'Ali was given the banner and captured a key fort; the people agreed to stay and farm the land for half the produce.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): Khaybar lay about 150 km north of Madina; exiled Banu al-Nadir leaders there had helped gather the confederates against Madina and continued to threaten it; in 7 AH, after Hudaybiyya, the Prophet (pbuh) marched with about 1,600 men; they arrived at night and attacked at dawn; there were several forts, taken one at a time; at the fort of al-Qamus the Prophet (pbuh) said he would give the banner to a man who loved God and His Messenger and whom they loved; he gave it to 'Ali, who captured the fort; Marhab, a famous warrior, was killed; the people asked to stay as farmers and give half their harvest; a woman tried to poison the Prophet (pbuh) with a cooked sheep; Ja'far and the Muslims from Abyssinia arrived at this time; Safiyya was married to the Prophet (pbuh). Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why do you think the Prophet (pbuh) allowed the people of Khaybar to stay and farm their land after the victory? Explain.
parts.answer: It was merciful and practical: they were skilled farmers, the land stayed productive, and people kept their homes and religion, which showed Islam's fairness.
parts.working: Points may include: mercy to a defeated people; they knew the land best; food supply for both sides; they kept their religion; justice in the division (a fair half share); shows war was not for destruction; lesson for treatment of defeated people today. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the month and year AH of the Battle of Badr, and name the place's main feature that the Muslims took control of.
parts.answer: Ramadan, 2 AH; the wells (water) of Badr.
parts.working: 1 mark for Ramadan 2 AH; 1 mark for the wells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Muslim army at Badr numbered about 313 and the Makkan army about 1,000. How many times larger was the Makkan army? Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: About 3.2 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the Prophet (pbuh) treated the prisoners of Badr.
parts.answer: He ordered them to be treated well; Companions fed them before themselves; ransom was accepted; literate prisoners who could not pay could earn freedom by teaching ten Muslim children to read and write.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: prisoners distributed among Companions to look after; told to treat them kindly; some Companions gave the prisoners bread and ate dates themselves; he consulted Abu Bakr and 'Umar on what to do; ransom accepted from families; poor prisoners released without ransom; literate prisoners taught ten children to read and write to earn freedom.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why releasing prisoners in return for teaching children shows the importance of education in Islam.
parts.answer: Teaching literacy was valued as highly as money, showing that knowledge is a priority for the Muslim community.
parts.working: 1 mark for knowledge valued as a ransom equal to money; 1 mark for development, e.g. first revelation 'Read', investment in the community's future.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the preparations for the expedition to Tabuk and how different Companions contributed.
parts.answer: In 9 AH in great heat the Prophet (pbuh) announced the expedition openly; 'Uthman equipped a large part of the army; Abu Bakr gave all he had; 'Umar gave half his wealth; poor Companions who had no mounts wept at being unable to go.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: reports of a Byzantine threat in the north; the season was very hot, harvest time and distance long; unusually the destination was announced openly; the army was called the 'army of hardship'; 'Uthman gave hundreds of camels and much gold; Abu Bakr brought all his wealth; 'Umar brought half of his; women gave jewellery; poor men who could not be given mounts wept (Sura 9.92); hypocrites made excuses to stay behind.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can Muslims today show the same generosity when their community faces an emergency, such as a flood? Explain.
parts.answer: By giving money, time, goods and skills according to their means, quickly and sincerely, as the Companions did.
parts.working: Points may include: donating to relief funds; volunteering; giving even small amounts like the poor Companions; sincerity, not for show; organising collections at school or mosque; full marks for development with example. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the Battle of Uhud.
parts.answer: In 3 AH the Quraysh came with about 3,000 men to avenge Badr; the Prophet (pbuh) consulted and went out; 'Abdullah bin Ubayy withdrew with about 300, leaving about 700 Muslims; 50 archers under 'Abdullah bin Jubayr were placed on a hill and told not to leave; the Muslims were winning, but most archers left their post to collect spoils; Khalid bin al-Walid led cavalry around the hill and attacked from behind; the Muslims were thrown into confusion; Hamza was martyred by Wahshi; the Prophet (pbuh) was wounded and a rumour spread that he had been killed; about 70 Muslims were martyred.
parts.working: Indicative content: Date (3 AH / 625); Quraysh about 3,000 seeking revenge for Badr; consultation, decision to fight outside the city; withdrawal of 'Abdullah bin Ubayy and about 300; about 700 Muslims; 50 archers on the hill under 'Abdullah bin Jubayr; instruction not to leave whatever happened; early Muslim success; archers left their post; Khalid bin al-Walid's attack from behind; Hamza martyred (by Wahshi); the Prophet (pbuh) wounded / rumour of his death; about 70 martyrs including Mus'ab bin 'Umayr. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What lesson did the Muslims learn about obedience at Uhud? Explain how it applies today.
parts.answer: Disobeying clear instructions for personal gain can harm the whole community, so Muslims should follow rightful leadership and rules even when tempted.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Lesson (archers' disobedience caused the setback), a modern application (e.g. following safety rules at work or a team plan). Model answer: Disobeying clear instructions for personal gain can harm the whole community, so Muslims should follow rightful leadership and rules even when tempted. Marked by levels out of 4. Level 4 (4): a well-developed, reasoned answer (two developed points, or one fully developed point) linked to life today, with a clear judgement where the question asks for one. Level 3 (3): a reasoned answer with some development and a relevant example, but the judgement or link to today is less clear. Level 2 (2): one or two simple points with little development. Level 1 (1): a basic, general statement. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Battle of the Trench (Khandaq).
parts.answer: In 5 AH a confederate army of about 10,000 from the Quraysh and allied tribes marched on Madina; on Salman al-Farsi's advice the Muslims, about 3,000, dug a trench on the open northern side, with the Prophet (pbuh) digging alongside them; the enemy could not cross and besieged the city for several weeks; the Jewish tribe of Banu Qurayza broke their agreement, creating danger from inside; 'Ali killed the champion 'Amr bin 'Abd Wudd in single combat; disagreement was sown among the enemy and a fierce cold wind and storm destroyed their camp, so they withdrew.
parts.working: Indicative content: 5 AH / 627; confederates (al-Ahzab) about 10,000; Muslims about 3,000; trench suggested by Salman al-Farsi (a Persian method); the Prophet (pbuh) worked with the Companions in hunger and cold; siege of several weeks; Banu Qurayza broke their treaty; duel — 'Ali killed 'Amr bin 'Abd Wudd; division sown among the enemy (Nu'aym bin Mas'ud); violent wind / storm; enemy withdrew without taking Madina. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what Muslims can learn from the way the Prophet (pbuh) accepted Salman's suggestion.
parts.answer: Good leaders consult others and accept good ideas from anyone, whatever their background, and work alongside their people.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Consultation (shura) is part of Islamic leadership; merit not origin — Salman was a Persian convert; example today, e.g. a company manager or school head welcoming ideas from staff and students. Model answer: Good leaders consult others and accept good ideas from anyone, whatever their background, and work alongside their people. Marked by levels out of 4. Level 4 (4): a well-developed, reasoned answer (two developed points, or one fully developed point) linked to life today, with a clear judgement where the question asks for one. Level 3 (3): a reasoned answer with some development and a relevant example, but the judgement or link to today is less clear. Level 2 (2): one or two simple points with little development. Level 1 (1): a basic, general statement. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Muslims fought battles during the Prophet's (pbuh) time in Madina, referring to what the Qur'an says about permission to fight.
parts.answer: Permission came because they had been wronged and driven from their homes (Sura 22.39–40); battles were to defend the community and Madina, protect freedom of religion and respond to aggression and broken treaties, within strict limits.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): in Makka Muslims were told to be patient and not fight back; after the Hijra, Sura 22.39–40 gave permission to those who were wronged and driven from their homes; the Quraysh continued hostility and seized Muslim property; Madina was attacked or threatened (Uhud, the Trench); fighting was to defend religious freedom so that people could worship God; treaties broken by others led to action (e.g. conquest of Makka); limits: do not transgress (2.190), stop if the enemy stops; no harm to women, children, the elderly or monks; peace to be accepted when offered (8.61); most expeditions ended without fighting. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some people claim Islam spread by the sword. Using the Prophet's (pbuh) life, explain how a Muslim might answer this.
parts.answer: The Qur'an says there is no compulsion in religion (2.256); most conversions happened during peace (after Hudaybiyya) and through preaching and character; battles were defensive and few lives were lost.
parts.working: Points may include: 2.256 no compulsion; Makka was conquered almost without bloodshed and people were not forced to convert; numbers increased greatly in the Hudaybiyya peace; Islam later spread to Indonesia and parts of Africa through traders; total deaths in the Prophet's battles were small; a reasoned answer for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: About 1,000 men set out from Madina towards Uhud, but 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy turned back with about 300. How many men remained with the Prophet (pbuh)?
parts.answer: About 700

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of the archers at Uhud and what happened when they left their position.
parts.answer: About 50 archers under 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr were posted on a hill and told never to leave it; when the Makkans began to retreat most left to collect booty; Khalid ibn al-Walid led cavalry round the hill and attacked from behind, turning victory into heavy losses.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: about 50 archers placed on a small hill (Jabal al-Rumat / 'Aynayn); commanded by 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr; ordered not to leave whatever happened; the Muslims were winning at first; most archers left to gather spoils; their commander and a few stayed and were killed; Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry attacked from behind; panic, rumour that the Prophet (pbuh) had been killed; he was wounded; about 70 Muslims were martyred, including Hamza.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the lesson of the archers could apply to a member of a team in a modern workplace or sports team.
parts.answer: Following the agreed plan and the leader's instructions matters more than personal gain; one person leaving their role can cause the whole team to fail.
parts.working: 1 mark for discipline/obedience to the agreed plan; 1 mark for not chasing personal reward (greed); 1 mark for a relevant example (e.g. a defender leaving position in a match, a security guard leaving a post).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the instructions the Prophet (pbuh) gave about how Muslims must behave in war.
parts.answer: Do not kill women, children, the elderly or religious people in their places of worship; do not mutilate bodies; do not betray or break promises; do not destroy crops, trees or animals needlessly; treat prisoners well.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: not to kill women or children; not to kill the old or those who do not fight; leave monks and worshippers alone; no mutilation of the dead; no treachery; no cutting fruit trees or burning crops without need; no killing animals except for food; accept peace if offered; treat prisoners humanely.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these rules compare with modern ideas of the protection of civilians in war.
parts.answer: They anticipated modern humanitarian law, which also protects civilians, prisoners and property, showing that Islam set limits on war centuries earlier.
parts.working: Points may include: modern laws such as the Geneva Conventions protect civilians and prisoners; Islamic rules did this in the 7th century; both forbid targeting non-combatants; both protect places of worship; Muslims today must obey these rules, and their breach by anyone is wrong; an evaluative comment earns full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the siege of Ta'if after the Battle of Hunayn and how the people of Ta'if later came to Islam.
parts.answer: After Hunayn (8 AH) the Thaqif retreated into fortified Ta'if; the Muslims besieged it for some weeks but it held out; the Prophet (pbuh) lifted the siege and prayed for their guidance rather than against them; he returned the Hawazin captives; in 9 AH a delegation from Thaqif came to Madina and accepted Islam, and their idol al-Lat was destroyed.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): the Thaqif and Hawazin had fought at Hunayn; the Thaqif shut themselves in walled Ta'if; the Muslims besieged it, some were killed by arrows; it was strongly defended with supplies; the Prophet (pbuh) consulted and decided to lift the siege; asked to curse them he prayed instead for their guidance; at al-Ji'rana he distributed the spoils of Hunayn, giving generously to new Muslims; on the Hawazin's request he returned their captives; Malik ibn 'Awf, the Hawazin leader, accepted Islam; in 9 AH a Thaqif delegation came to Madina; they accepted Islam; they asked to keep their idol for a time but this was refused; al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba and Abu Sufyan were sent to destroy al-Lat. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Years earlier the people of Ta'if had stoned the Prophet (pbuh). What does his treatment of them now teach Muslims about holding grudges?
parts.answer: He prayed for them instead of taking revenge, showing that forgiveness and patience can win hearts; Muslims should not hold grudges.
parts.working: Points may include: he could have destroyed them twice but did not; he prayed for their guidance; they later became loyal Muslims; forgiveness is stronger than revenge; applying this in family or school quarrels; full marks for reasoned link to today. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the expedition to Tabuk.
parts.answer: In 9 AH, on news that the Byzantines were gathering forces in the north, the Prophet (pbuh) called for an expedition in intense summer heat at harvest time; Companions gave generously — 'Uthman equipped a large part of the army, Abu Bakr gave all his wealth and 'Umar half of his; about 30,000 marched; the hypocrites made excuses and stayed behind; at Tabuk no enemy appeared; the Prophet (pbuh) stayed some days and made agreements with local tribes; Ka'b bin Malik and two others who stayed behind without excuse were boycotted until God accepted their repentance.
parts.working: Indicative content: 9 AH / 630; Byzantine threat; extreme heat, long distance, harvest time; appeal for funds; 'Uthman's large contribution; Abu Bakr gave everything; 'Umar gave half; army about 30,000; hypocrites' excuses; no battle took place; treaties with local tribes / show of strength; Ka'b bin Malik and two others boycotted and later forgiven. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What does this expedition teach Muslims about sincerity in difficult times? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: True faith shows when sacrifice is hard: the sincere gave wealth and effort despite heat and harvest, while hypocrites made excuses; Ka'b's honesty about his failure shows truthfulness brings forgiveness.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Sacrifice reveals sincerity; contrast with hypocrites' excuses; Ka'b's honesty rather than lying — applied today, e.g. admitting a mistake at work. Model answer: True faith shows when sacrifice is hard: the sincere gave wealth and effort despite heat and harvest, while hypocrites made excuses; Ka'b's honesty about his failure shows truthfulness brings forgiveness. Level 3 (3): a reasoned answer with some development and a relevant example, but the judgement or link to today is less clear. Level 2 (2): one or two simple points with little development. Level 1 (1): a basic, general statement. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Battle of Hunayn.
parts.answer: In 8 AH, soon after the conquest of Makka, the Hawazin and Thaqif tribes gathered to attack; the Muslims marched with about 12,000 men, and some felt sure of victory because of their numbers; the enemy ambushed them in a narrow valley at dawn and many Muslims fled; the Prophet (pbuh) stood firm with a few Companions and al-'Abbas called the others back; they regrouped and won; large amounts of spoils and captives were taken, and later the captives were returned when the Hawazin accepted Islam.
parts.working: Indicative content: 8 AH, after the conquest of Makka; enemies — Hawazin and Thaqif; Muslims about 12,000, including new Muslims from Makka; overconfidence in numbers (mentioned in the Qur'an, Sura 9); ambush in the valley of Hunayn; Muslims fled in confusion; the Prophet (pbuh) stood firm; al-'Abbas called the Companions back; victory; much booty; generosity to new Muslims / captives returned. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare the lessons of Badr and Hunayn about numbers and victory.
parts.answer: At Badr a small, faithful army won; at Hunayn a large army nearly lost through overconfidence; together they teach that victory comes from God and reliance on Him, not from size or resources.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Badr — few but trusting in God; Hunayn — many but proud, near defeat; conclusion applied today, e.g. not relying only on wealth or connections but on effort and trust in God. Model answer: At Badr a small, faithful army won; at Hunayn a large army nearly lost through overconfidence; together they teach that victory comes from God and reliance on Him, not from size or resources. Marked by levels out of 4. Level 3 (3): a reasoned answer with some development and a relevant example, but the judgement or link to today is less clear. Level 2 (2): one or two simple points with little development. Level 1 (1): a basic, general statement. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the Battle of Mu'ta.
parts.answer: In 8 AH an army of about 3,000 was sent towards Syria after the Prophet's (pbuh) envoy was killed; it met a much larger Byzantine and allied force at Mu'ta; the three appointed commanders, Zayd ibn Haritha, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha, were martyred one after another; Khalid ibn al-Walid took command and withdrew the army safely.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): it happened in 8 AH (629 CE) in the south of present-day Jordan; cause: the Prophet's (pbuh) envoy al-Harith ibn 'Umayr was killed by a local ruler allied to the Byzantines; about 3,000 Muslims went; the Prophet (pbuh) named three commanders in order: Zayd ibn Haritha, then Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, then 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha; they met a very much larger force; Zayd was martyred, then Ja'far, who held the banner after losing both hands, then 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha; Khalid ibn al-Walid was chosen; he reorganised the lines and withdrew the army safely; the Prophet (pbuh) told the people of Madina of the deaths before news arrived and wept; he called Ja'far one who flies in Paradise with two wings (al-Tayyar); Khalid was called the 'Sword of God'. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some people in Madina called the returning army 'runaways'. Do you think the withdrawal from Mu'ta was a defeat? Give reasons.
parts.answer: Not really: saving an outnumbered army was a wise success; the Prophet (pbuh) defended them, and the battle showed Muslim courage to a great empire.
parts.working: Points may include: the army was greatly outnumbered; a safe withdrawal preserved lives for the future; the Prophet (pbuh) said they would return to fight again, not that they had fled; courage of commanders impressed Arab tribes; but the aim of punishing the killers was not achieved at once; balanced answer for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Muslims were successful at the Battle of the Trench (Khandaq), even though very little fighting took place.
parts.answer: The trench stopped the large confederate army; Muslims dug it together quickly and guarded it; the alliance of enemies was broken by distrust (through Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud's efforts); a fierce cold wind and God's help ended the siege; the enemy lacked supplies and left.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): in 5 AH a confederate army of about 10,000 came to destroy Madina; Salman al-Farisi suggested a trench, a method unknown to the Arabs; the Muslims, including the Prophet (pbuh), dug it quickly in cold and hunger; it blocked the open northern side while other sides were protected by hills, lava fields and palm groves; cavalry could not cross; a few riders, including 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wudd, crossed and 'Ali killed him in single combat; the siege lasted weeks and the enemy ran short of food and fodder; Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, a new Muslim, secretly created mistrust between the Quraysh, Ghatafan and Banu Qurayza; a violent cold wind blew over the enemy camp, knocking down tents and putting out fires (Sura 33.9 speaks of a wind and hosts you did not see); Abu Sufyan ordered withdrawal; the Prophet (pbuh) said that from now on the Muslims would go to them, not they to the Muslims. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which do you think was more important in the Muslims' success: human planning or God's help? Give reasons.
parts.answer: Both worked together: the trench and diplomacy were wise efforts, but the wind and the breakdown of the alliance were seen as God's help; Muslims are taught to plan and then trust God.
parts.working: Points may include: planning: trench, guarding, Nu'aym's work; God's help: wind, unseen hosts (33.9), fear in enemy hearts; Islam teaches effort plus trust (tawakkul); an argued judgement with examples for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the Battles of Badr and Uhud: their causes, the numbers involved, the course of events and the results.
parts.answer: Badr (2 AH): about 313 Muslims beat about 1,000 Makkans after the Makkans marched to protect a caravan; a decisive Muslim victory. Uhud (3 AH): about 700 Muslims against about 3,000 Makkans who came for revenge; early success turned to heavy losses after the archers left their post.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): Badr: caused by the Quraysh coming to defend Abu Sufyan's caravan; Ramadan 2 AH; about 313 Muslims with few horses and camels against about 1,000; Muslims held the wells; single combats at the start (Hamza, 'Ali, 'Ubayda); help of angels (8.9); about 70 Makkans killed including Abu Jahl and 14 Muslims martyred; prisoners ransomed. Uhud: 3 AH, the Quraysh came for revenge for Badr; about 3,000 Makkans; Ibn Ubayy withdrew 300 so about 700 Muslims; archers posted on a hill; Muslims winning, archers left; Khalid's attack from behind; about 70 Muslims martyred, including Hamza; Prophet (pbuh) wounded; Makkans did not take Madina; comparison: Badr raised Muslim morale, Uhud taught obedience and patience (Sura 3). Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Uhud taught the Muslims more than Badr did.' How far do you agree? Give reasons.
parts.answer: Arguments both ways: Badr proved that faith and unity outweigh numbers; Uhud taught obedience, the danger of greed and patience in setback; a reasoned judgement is required.
parts.working: Points may include: Badr: confidence, God's help to the faithful, treatment of prisoners; Uhud: obedience, discipline, sincerity, dealing with defeat; Qur'an commentary in Sura 3 on Uhud; lessons from defeat often last longer; justified conclusion for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Conquest of Makka and final years

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give an account of the conquest of Makka.
parts.answer: In 8 AH, after allies of the Quraysh (Banu Bakr) attacked the Banu Khuza'a, allies of the Muslims, the Treaty of Hudaybiyya was broken; the Prophet (pbuh) marched with about 10,000 men; at camp outside Makka Abu Sufyan came and accepted Islam; the Prophet (pbuh) announced that anyone who stayed in Abu Sufyan's house, in their own home or in the Sacred Mosque was safe; the army entered Makka with almost no fighting; the Prophet (pbuh) entered humbly; he cleared the Ka'ba of about 360 idols, reciting that truth had come and falsehood vanished; Bilal called the adhan from the Ka'ba; he pardoned the people of Makka, saying there was no blame on them that day.
parts.working: Indicative content: Breach of Hudaybiyya (Banu Bakr against Banu Khuza'a); Abu Sufyan's failed attempt to renew the treaty; 10,000 Muslims; Ramadan 8 AH / 630; camp fires at Marr al-Zahran; Abu Sufyan's acceptance of Islam; amnesty conditions (his house, own homes, the Haram); entry from several directions, little resistance; the Prophet (pbuh) entered with head bowed in humility; idols destroyed (Sura 17.81 recited); Bilal's adhan on the Ka'ba; general pardon, even of former enemies. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What does the Prophet's (pbuh) treatment of the people of Makka teach Muslims today?
parts.answer: To forgive enemies when in a position of power, rather than taking revenge.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Lesson, a modern application (e.g. forgiving a relative who wronged you, or reconciliation after conflict). practice.subtopic: Conquest of Makka and final years

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the Treaty of Hudaybiyya was broken and what happened before the Muslim army set out for Makka.
parts.answer: The Banu Bakr, allies of the Quraysh, attacked the Khuza'a, allies of the Muslims, with Quraysh help; the Khuza'a asked the Prophet (pbuh) for help; Abu Sufyan came to Madina to renew the treaty but failed; the Prophet (pbuh) prepared an army secretly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: under the treaty tribes could ally with either side; Banu Bakr joined the Quraysh and Khuza'a joined the Muslims; in 8 AH Banu Bakr attacked Khuza'a at night, some Quraysh helping with weapons and men; some Khuza'a were killed even in the sacred area; 'Amr ibn Salim of Khuza'a rode to Madina to ask for help; Abu Sufyan travelled to Madina to repair the treaty but no one would support him; the Prophet (pbuh) prepared an army and kept the destination secret.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Prophet (pbuh) kept the march to Makka secret.
parts.answer: To take Makka by surprise so the Quraysh had no time to prepare to fight, which avoided bloodshed in the sacred city.
parts.working: Points may include: surprise prevented a battle; protecting lives on both sides; preserving the sanctity of the Haram; he prayed that the news would not reach the Quraysh; a letter sent by a Companion to warn Makka was intercepted; shows wise strategy aimed at peace. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Conquest of Makka and final years

parts.label: a
parts.text: State: (i) the year AH of the conquest of Makka; (ii) the approximate size of the Muslim army; (iii) the Companion who gave the call to prayer from the Ka'ba.
parts.answer: (i) 8 AH (ii) about 10,000 (iii) Bilal
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Prophet (pbuh) left Makka in 622 CE and conquered it in 630 CE. How many years after the Hijra did he return as conqueror?
parts.answer: 8 years

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the conquest of Makka changed Arabia.
parts.answer: The Ka'ba was cleansed of idols so the centre of Arab religion became the centre of tawhid; the Quraysh's opposition ended, so many tribes now accepted Islam and sent delegations.
parts.working: 2 marks for each explained change (1 identify + 1 develop): idol worship lost its centre; Quraysh, leaders of Arab opinion, accepted Islam; tribes joined in large numbers (Sura 110); Muslims could perform hajj freely; peace across most of Arabia.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the Prophet (pbuh) did in his last days to prepare the community for life after his death.
parts.answer: He appointed Abu Bakr to lead the prayers, gave final advice about prayer and treating slaves and women well, gave away his remaining money, asked people to forgive him if he had wronged anyone, and ordered Usama's army to set out.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: illness began after visiting al-Baqi' cemetery; he stayed in 'A'isha's room with the permission of his wives; he asked Abu Bakr to lead the prayers; he addressed the people, asking anyone he had wronged to claim their right; he praised Abu Bakr's service; he urged care for the Ansar; he advised guarding the prayer and kindness to slaves and those under one's care; he gave away the few coins he had; he insisted Usama ibn Zayd's army be sent; he died in 11 AH (632 CE).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Prophet's (pbuh) request to settle any wrongs before he died is a lesson for Muslims.
parts.answer: It shows that rights of people must be settled in this life, not left to the Day of Judgement, and that even a leader is accountable.
parts.working: Points may include: people's rights are not forgiven by God unless the wronged person forgives; returning debts and apologising; humility of the greatest person; leaders are accountable; making a will and paying debts before death. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the events at the Saqifa of Banu Sa'ida after the Prophet's (pbuh) death, and how Abu Bakr came to be chosen as the first caliph.
parts.answer: The Ansar met at the Saqifa of Banu Sa'ida and put forward Sa'd ibn 'Ubada; Abu Bakr, 'Umar and Abu 'Ubayda reminded them that leadership belonged to the Quraysh, and after debate 'Umar pledged to Abu Bakr; the people followed and Abu Bakr was accepted as the first caliph, while some, including 'Ali, delayed their pledge for a time.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): the Prophet (pbuh) died in 11 AH while his family prepared his burial; the Ansar gathered at the Saqifa of Banu Sa'ida to choose a leader from among themselves; Sa'd ibn 'Ubada was put forward; Abu Bakr, 'Umar and Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah argued that leadership belonged to the Quraysh, citing the Prophet's words; 'Umar gave the first pledge to Abu Bakr and the people followed; a public pledge was given in the mosque the next day; Abu Bakr's first address stressed that Muhammad was a man who had died and that God is alive; some, including 'Ali and Banu Hashim, delayed; a balanced account of the debate and the consensus earns full marks. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the choice of Abu Bakr through the agreement of the community was important for the future of the Muslim community.
parts.answer: It settled leadership quickly and avoided a split at a time of grief, and it showed that leadership rests on the community's agreement; the principle was later debated, since some supporters of 'Ali argued for a different basis.
parts.working: Points may include: a peaceful transfer avoided civil strife at a time of grief; consultation and agreement as the basis for choosing a leader; Abu Bakr's close companionship and trust; later disagreement over 'Ali's claim, so a balanced answer notes differing views; a reasoned answer with a relevant example for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main teachings of the Prophet's (pbuh) Farewell Sermon.
parts.answer: Delivered during the Farewell Pilgrimage in 10 AH at 'Arafat: the lives, property and honour of Muslims are sacred; interest (usury) is abolished; blood feuds from the time of ignorance are ended; husbands and wives have rights over each other and women must be treated kindly; all humans descend from Adam, and no Arab is better than a non-Arab, nor white than black, except by piety; Muslims are brothers; perform prayer, fasting, zakat and hajj; he left the Qur'an (and his guidance) to hold on to; those present should pass on the message.
parts.working: Indicative content: Setting — Farewell Hajj, 10 AH, plain of 'Arafat; sanctity of life, property and honour; usury abolished; blood revenge of pre-Islamic times ended; rights of women and kindness to wives; rights of husbands; equality of all races — superiority only by piety; brotherhood of Muslims; do not wrong others / return trusts; carry out the pillars; hold to the Qur'an and the Sunna; convey the message to those absent; he asked whether he had conveyed the message and called God to witness. parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the last illness and death of the Prophet (pbuh) and how the Muslims reacted.
parts.answer: In 11 AH (632 CE), soon after the Farewell Pilgrimage, he fell ill with fever and headache; with his wives' agreement he stayed in 'A'isha's room; he continued to advise the Muslims, especially about prayer and kind treatment of those under their care; he died at about the age of 63; many Companions were shocked and 'Umar at first refused to believe it; Abu Bakr reminded the people that whoever worshipped Muhammad should know he had died, but God is alive and never dies, and recited the verse that Muhammad is only a messenger (Sura 3.144); his family, including 'Ali and al-'Abbas, washed his body, and he was buried in the room where he died.

parts.text: Why do you think Abu Bakr's words after the Prophet's (pbuh) death were important?
parts.answer: They calmed the community, reminded people that the Prophet (pbuh) was a human messenger and that worship belongs to God alone, and kept Muslims united at a dangerous moment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the Prophet (pbuh) did inside Makka on the day of its conquest, from his entry to the Ka'ba until he spoke to the people of Makka.
parts.answer: He entered humbly with head bowed, performed tawaf, destroyed the 360 idols around the Ka'ba reciting 'Truth has come and falsehood has vanished' (17.81), cleansed the Ka'ba of images, had Bilal give the adhan from its roof, returned its key to 'Uthman ibn Talha and announced a general pardon to the Quraysh.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): the army of about 10,000 entered from several directions with orders not to fight unless attacked; he rode in with his head bowed so low it almost touched his camel; he went to the Ka'ba and performed tawaf; about 360 idols stood around it; he struck them with a stick and they fell while he recited 17.81; images inside the Ka'ba were removed; he prayed inside; Bilal climbed onto the Ka'ba and called the adhan; he gave the key back to 'Uthman ibn Talha and his family; he asked the Quraysh what they expected and they said good from a noble brother; he told them there was no blame on them that day and they were free; property and blood feuds of the time of ignorance were cancelled; people pledged allegiance. parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Prophet (pbuh) gave the key of the Ka'ba back to its old keepers instead of keeping it for his own family.
parts.answer: To fulfil a trust (Sura 4.58 tells believers to return trusts to their owners), keep established duties, show he did not want privilege, and win hearts.
parts.working: Points may include: 4.58 return trusts to whom they are due; avoided accusations of seeking power for his clan; respected long-standing roles; showed fairness to a former opponent; lesson for leaders not to give posts to relatives without merit. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pilgrimage of 9 AH, led by Abu Bakr, and the announcement made during it.
parts.answer: The Prophet (pbuh) sent Abu Bakr to lead the hajj; 'Ali was sent to announce the opening verses of Sura 9 (al-Tawba/Bara'a); it was declared that after that year no idolater would make the pilgrimage and no one would circle the Ka'ba naked; existing treaties would be honoured until their end.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: in 9 AH the Prophet (pbuh) stayed in Madina; Abu Bakr was appointed leader of the hajj; 'Ali followed to recite the opening part of Sura 9; idolaters were given a period of four months; treaties kept with those who had kept them would be honoured to their term; from the following year no idolater would perform hajj; tawaf without clothes, an old custom, was banned; this prepared for the Farewell Pilgrimage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why was it important to purify the rituals of hajj before the Prophet (pbuh) performed his own pilgrimage?
parts.answer: So that the hajj he performed and taught would be pure worship of God as in Ibrahim's time, free of idolatrous customs, giving Muslims a correct model.
parts.working: Points may include: hajj restored to its origin with Ibrahim; removal of pagan practices; the Prophet's (pbuh) hajj became the example for all later Muslims; ensured unity of practice; links to the Ka'ba as house of tawhid. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Conquest of Makka and final years

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give an account of the Farewell Pilgrimage in 10 AH (do not describe the sermon in detail).
parts.answer: The Prophet (pbuh) announced he would make hajj, and very large numbers joined him; he entered ihram at Dhu al-Hulayfa, performed tawaf and sa'y, went to Mina and Arafat where he gave his sermon and where Sura 5.3 was revealed, stayed at Muzdalifa, stoned at Mina, sacrificed and shaved, teaching the rites as he went.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): 10 AH; the only hajj he performed after the Hijra; announced in advance; people came from all over Arabia, a huge crowd; he put on ihram at Dhu al-Hulayfa near Madina and recited the talbiya; arrived in Makka, performed tawaf and sa'y; on 8 Dhu al-Hijja went to Mina; on 9 went to Arafat and gave his sermon from his camel at the plain; revelation of 5.3, that the religion had been perfected; spent the night at Muzdalifa; on 10 stoned the pillar at Mina, sacrificed animals and shaved his head; tawaf al-ifada; stayed in Mina for the days of tashriq; told people to learn their rites from him, as he might not meet them again; called it a farewell. parts.text: Why do you think the revelation that the religion had been 'perfected' was received with both joy and sadness by some Companions?
parts.answer: Joy because Islam was complete; sadness because some, such as Abu Bakr, understood that the Prophet's (pbuh) mission was finishing and his death was near.
parts.working: Points may include: completion of guidance is a blessing; once a task is complete, the messenger's time ends; Abu Bakr and others wept; the Prophet (pbuh) died about three months later; full marks for both feelings explained. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Conquest of Makka and final years

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the Prophet (pbuh) taught in his Farewell Sermon about (i) the equality of all people and (ii) property and money.
parts.answer: (i) All people come from Adam; no Arab is better than a non-Arab, nor a white person than a black person, except by piety. (ii) The lives and property of Muslims are sacred; usury (riba) of the time of ignorance was cancelled, starting with that of al-'Abbas; trusts must be returned.
parts.working: 2 marks for each of (i) and (ii): (i) all humans descend from Adam; no superiority of Arab over non-Arab or of colour over colour; only taqwa/piety distinguishes; all Muslims are brothers. (ii) life, property and honour sacred like that day and month; riba abolished, beginning with his uncle al-'Abbas's dues; return trusts; take only what is given willingly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A company in Lahore pays workers from one ethnic group more than others for the same job. Using the sermon, explain what a Muslim manager should do.
parts.answer: Pay everyone equally for equal work, because the sermon forbids superiority by race or origin and protects people's rights to their property and wages.
parts.working: Points may include: equality of all people regardless of ethnicity; unfair pay is taking others' rights (property sacred); justice is a duty of those in authority; speak to owners, change policy; reward based on effort and merit; good example for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Conquest of Makka and final years

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Year of Delegations (9 AH) and how the Prophet (pbuh) dealt with the delegations that came to Madina.
parts.answer: After the conquest of Makka, the victory at Hunayn and the expedition to Tabuk, tribes from all over Arabia sent delegations to Madina, so 9 AH became known as the Year of Delegations; the Prophet (pbuh) received them in his mosque, treated them as honoured guests and gave them gifts; the Thaqif of Ta'if accepted Islam, but their requests to keep their idol al-Lat for a time and to be excused from prayer were refused; the Christians of Najran discussed their beliefs with him, were allowed to pray in the mosque and made a treaty that let them keep their faith; teachers and officials were sent back with many tribes; Sura 110 describes people entering God's religion in crowds; in the same year Abu Bakr led the Hajj.
parts.working: Indicative content: 9 AH called the Year of Delegations ('Am al-Wufud); followed the conquest of Makka, Hunayn and Tabuk; delegations from across Arabia; received in the mosque with honour and gifts; Thaqif accepted Islam; their requests to keep al-Lat / be excused from prayer refused; Christians of Najran — discussion, allowed to pray in the mosque, treaty letting them keep their religion; teachers / officials sent with tribes; Sura 110 (people entering Islam in crowds); Abu Bakr led the Hajj of 9 AH.
