practice.subtopic: Migration and the move to Madina

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the hardships faced by Companions who migrated from Makka to Madina before or around the time of the Prophet (pbuh), referring to individuals such as Abu Salama and Umm Salama, Suhayb al-Rumi and 'Umar.
parts.answer: Abu Salama's family were separated by their clans and Umm Salama waited about a year before travelling with her son; Suhayb gave up all his wealth to the Quraysh in exchange for being allowed to leave; 'Umar left openly, challenging anyone to stop him; others were imprisoned or tricked into returning; all left homes and property behind.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): the Prophet (pbuh) allowed Muslims to migrate after the second pledge; most left secretly in small groups; Abu Salama set out with his wife and baby; her clan Banu Mughira took her back; his clan Banu 'Abd al-Asad took the child; Abu Salama went on alone; Umm Salama wept daily for about a year; finally reunited with her son, she set off alone and 'Uthman ibn Talha, not then Muslim, escorted her to Quba; Suhayb, a wealthy Roman-born trader, was stopped; he gave his wealth in exchange for leaving; the Prophet (pbuh) said his trade had profited; 'Umar circled the Ka'ba and openly announced his departure, daring anyone to stop him; 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a was tricked into returning and imprisoned; Muslims lost houses, businesses and families; the Muhajirun arrived poor. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The sacrifices of the early Muslims during the Hijra have lessons for refugees and migrants today.' Discuss.
parts.answer: Yes: they show patience, faith and courage in leaving home, and the Ansar's welcome is a model for host communities; but modern migrants often move for different reasons, so care is needed in comparison.
parts.working: Points may include: patience and trust in God; family separation; generosity of host communities (Ansar); duty to help refugees, e.g. Afghan refugees in Pakistan; migrants should contribute to their new societies; difference between religious hijra and economic migration; balanced conclusion for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Migration and the move to Madina

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the people of Yathrib were ready to accept Islam and invite the Prophet (pbuh) to their town.
parts.answer: Long civil war between the Aws and Khazraj, ending at Bu'ath, left them needing a neutral leader; Jewish neighbours spoke of an expected prophet, so they recognised the signs; they had links with the Prophet's (pbuh) family (his great-grandfather's wife and his mother's relatives); Mus'ab taught them; they were less tied to the Makkan idol trade.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): the Aws and Khazraj had fought for many years; the Battle of Bu'ath (about 617 CE) left many leaders dead and both sides exhausted; they needed an outside arbiter respected by all; Jewish tribes in Yathrib often spoke of a coming prophet, so the visitors at 'Aqaba recognised him; family ties: his grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib's mother was from Banu al-Najjar of Yathrib; his father was buried there and his mother visited relatives there; Yathrib's people did not have the Quraysh's economic interest in the Ka'ba's idols; the men who met him at 'Aqaba carried the message home; Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr's teaching; conversion of leaders like Sa'd ibn Mu'adh; the pledges gave a formal promise of protection. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which of these reasons do you think was most important? Give reasons for your choice.
parts.answer: Any reasoned choice, e.g. the need for peace after Bu'ath, since a leader who could unite both tribes was what the town most needed; full marks for justification and comparison.
parts.working: Points may include: argued choice; comparison with at least one other reason; recognise that religious conviction was also essential; examples from the pledges. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Migration and the move to Madina

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Prophet (pbuh) is reported to have taught that the true emigrant (muhajir) is the one who leaves what God has forbidden. Explain the meaning of hijra in this wider sense.
parts.answer: Hijra is not only moving place; it is turning away from sin and bad habits towards obedience to God, which every Muslim can do anywhere and at any time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: literal hijra = migration for God's sake; inner hijra = leaving sins; it is open to everyone, even after the physical Hijra ended; examples: leaving lying, backbiting, bad company; it requires sacrifice like the first emigrants; intention matters (actions judged by intentions, which was said in connection with hijra).

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The inner hijra from sin is harder than leaving one's home.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
parts.answer: Arguments both ways: leaving home is a one-time huge loss, but leaving sin is a lifelong struggle against desire; a reasoned conclusion is needed.
parts.working: Points may include: physical hijra meant loss of wealth and family; inner hijra is continuous and private; temptations today (phones, peer pressure); the first emigrants did both; argued judgement for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the childhood of the Prophet (pbuh) up to the age of eight.
parts.answer: He was born in Makka around 570 CE, the Year of the Elephant; his father 'Abdullah had died before his birth; following Makkan custom he was given to a foster-mother, Halima al-Sa'diyya of the Banu Sa'd, in the desert, where her family was blessed with plenty; he returned to his mother Amina; when he was about six she died at al-Abwa' on the way back from Yathrib, and Umm Ayman brought him home; his grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib cared for him lovingly until he died when the boy was about eight; then his uncle Abu Talib took him in.
parts.working: Indicative content: Born in Makka, about 570 CE, Year of the Elephant; clan Banu Hashim of Quraysh; father 'Abdullah died before his birth; nursed by Halima al-Sa'diyya; desert life for health and pure Arabic; blessings for Halima's household; returned to Amina; Amina died at al-Abwa' when he was six; Umm Ayman brought him back; grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib's care; 'Abd al-Muttalib died when he was eight; uncle Abu Talib became guardian. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What can Muslims learn from the way the Prophet (pbuh) was cared for as an orphan?
parts.answer: Families and society have a duty to care for orphans with love and support, as his relatives did.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Lesson, a practical example (e.g. supporting orphan sponsorship or caring for a relative's orphaned child). Model answer: Families and society have a duty to care for orphans with love and support, as his relatives did. Marked by levels out of 4. Level 4 (4): a well-developed, reasoned answer (two developed points, or one fully developed point) linked to life today, with a clear judgement where the question asks for one. Level 3 (3): a reasoned answer with some development and a relevant example, but the judgement or link to today is less clear. Level 2 (2): one or two simple points with little development. Level 1 (1): a basic, general statement. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events of the Year of the Elephant, as mentioned in Sura 105.
parts.answer: Abraha, the Abyssinian ruler of Yemen, built a church at San'a and marched on Makka with an army and elephant(s) to destroy the Ka'ba; 'Abd al-Muttalib asked for his camels and said the House had its own Lord; the Makkans withdrew to the hills; the elephant would not advance; God sent flocks of birds that pelted the army with stones of baked clay, destroying it; the Prophet (pbuh) was born that year.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): Abraha governed Yemen for the Abyssinian king; he built a great church in San'a hoping to draw pilgrims from the Ka'ba; angered by an insult to it he marched on Makka; his army included at least one large elephant (Mahmud); his men seized camels, including 200 of 'Abd al-Muttalib's; 'Abd al-Muttalib went to Abraha and asked only for his camels, saying the House had a Lord who would protect it; the Quraysh withdrew to the mountains; the elephant knelt and would not move towards Makka; birds in flocks (ababil) threw stones of baked clay; the army was left like eaten straw (Sura 105); Abraha fled and died; the Arabs dated events by this year; the Prophet (pbuh) was born that year, about 570 CE. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many Muslims see a link between this event and the birth of the Prophet (pbuh).
parts.answer: God protected the Ka'ba, the house of tawhid, in the very year the Prophet (pbuh) who would restore it was born, showing divine preparation for his mission and raising the Quraysh's status.
parts.working: Points may include: protection of the Ka'ba for its future role; increased the respect of the Quraysh among Arabs, which later helped the message; sign of God's power; same year as his birth; the Makkans remembered it, so Sura 105 reminded them of a known event. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the time the Prophet (pbuh) spent with his foster-mother Halima in the desert.
parts.answer: It was a Makkan custom to send babies to Bedouin wet-nurses; Halima of Banu Sa'd took the orphan when others would not; her family experienced blessings (more milk, a healthier flock); he stayed with them about four or five years, learning pure Arabic and desert life; after an unusual event (the opening of his chest) she returned him to his mother.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: desert air thought healthier and Arabic purer; nurses preferred children with rich fathers so many refused an orphan; Halima took him having found no other baby; her camel and goats gave more milk and her family prospered; he stayed with Banu Sa'd until about age four or five; foster-brothers and sisters (e.g. al-Shayma'); the report of two figures in white opening his chest; Halima worried and returned him to Amina.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits the Prophet (pbuh) gained from growing up in the desert.
parts.answer: Pure and eloquent Arabic, which helped him communicate the message; physical strength and simple, patient character from desert life; knowledge of Bedouin ways, useful when dealing with tribes later.
parts.working: 2 marks for each benefit explained (identify + develop): eloquent Arabic; health and strength; simplicity and independence; understanding of nomadic tribes; experience of shepherding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Prophet (pbuh) was born in about 570 CE. His mother Amina died when he was about 6, and his grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib when he was about 8. In about which years CE did these two deaths happen?
parts.answer: Amina about 576 CE; 'Abd al-Muttalib about 578 CE.

parts.label: b
parts.text: He married Khadija at 25 and received the first revelation at 40. How many years had they been married when the first revelation came?
parts.answer: 15 years

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the place where Amina died and the uncle who took care of the Prophet (pbuh) after his grandfather's death.
parts.answer: Al-Abwa'; Abu Talib
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how being an orphan may have shaped the Prophet's (pbuh) later care for orphans and the weak.
parts.answer: He knew the pain of losing parents and depending on others, so he stressed kindness to orphans; Sura 93 reminds him that God sheltered him as an orphan.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: personal experience of loss; Sura 93.6, 9 links his orphanhood to caring for orphans; his teaching that the one who cares for an orphan will be close to him in Paradise / practical support of orphans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the work the Prophet (pbuh) did as a young man before his marriage.
parts.answer: He worked as a shepherd for the people of Makka for small wages, and later as a trader, travelling with caravans and becoming known for honesty in business.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: herded sheep as a boy/youth near Makka; worked for wages (a few coins); later joined trading caravans; traded for others such as Khadija; known as al-Amin and al-Sadiq; fair in buying and selling; he later said every prophet had herded sheep.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Prophet (pbuh) said that all prophets had herded sheep. Explain what qualities shepherding might develop that would help a leader.
parts.answer: Patience, responsibility, gentleness and watchfulness over the weak, which are the qualities a leader needs to guide people.
parts.working: Points may include: patience with slow animals; protecting the flock from danger; caring for the weakest; humility of simple work; time in nature for reflection; respect for honest labour. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Hilf al-Fudul (the Pact of the Virtuous) and the Prophet's (pbuh) part in it.
parts.answer: After a Yemeni trader was cheated by a Makkan leader, several Makkan clans met in the house of 'Abd Allah ibn Jud'an and swore to support anyone wronged in Makka until their rights were restored; the young Prophet (pbuh), about twenty, took part; they recovered the trader's goods; later he said he would answer such a call even in Islam.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: a trader from Zabid in Yemen sold goods to al-'As ibn Wa'il who refused to pay; he appealed publicly; leaders of several clans including Banu Hashim met at Ibn Jud'an's house; they pledged to stand with the oppressed, whether local or stranger; they forced the payment; the Prophet (pbuh) was about 20 and took part with his uncles; he later said he would not exchange his membership of it for red camels and would respond to such a call in Islam.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how young Muslims in Pakistan today could act on the spirit of this pact.
parts.answer: By standing up together for people who are cheated or bullied, supporting legal aid, consumer rights and anti-bullying efforts, regardless of the victim's background.
parts.working: Points may include: anti-bullying groups at school; helping someone cheated by a shopkeeper or employer; supporting charities that give legal help; speaking up for minorities and strangers; working with people of other faiths for justice (the pact was before Islam). 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give an account of the rebuilding of the Ka'ba when the Prophet (pbuh) was 35 and how he settled the dispute over the Black Stone.
parts.answer: The Ka'ba was damaged and the Quraysh rebuilt it using only lawful money; when the walls reached the Black Stone the clans argued over who would place it; they agreed the first person to enter the Haram would decide; it was the Prophet (pbuh); he put the Stone on a cloth, each clan leader held a corner and he placed it himself.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: the Ka'ba was damaged by flood/fire; the Quraysh rebuilt it, the Prophet (pbuh) carrying stones; only pure earnings were used, so the building was made smaller (Hatim area left outside); a fierce dispute over the honour of placing the Black Stone; near violence for days; Abu Umayya suggested the first person to enter decide; it was the Prophet (pbuh), welcomed as al-Amin; the cloth solution; each clan shared the honour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this event teaches about resolving conflicts between groups.
parts.answer: A trusted, fair person can find a solution that respects everyone's dignity; sharing honour avoids violence; creativity and fairness work better than force.
parts.working: Points may include: trustworthiness gives authority; solution let every group share; avoided bloodshed; listening to all sides; examples today: mediation between families or political parties. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about Khadija bint Khuwaylid's trade with the Prophet (pbuh) and their marriage.
parts.answer: Khadija was a wealthy, respected widow and trader; hearing of his honesty she employed him to lead a caravan to Syria with her servant Maysara; he made a large profit and Maysara praised his character; she proposed marriage through a friend; they married when he was 25 and she about 40; it was a happy marriage of about 25 years and they had six children.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): Khadija was a noble and wealthy Quraysh woman, a widow who hired men to trade for her; called al-Tahira (the pure); she heard of his reputation as al-Amin; she offered him more than her usual share to lead her caravan to Syria; Maysara travelled with him; he traded honestly and made a large profit; Maysara reported his good character; she sent a friend to ask whether he would marry; Abu Talib and her family agreed; he was 25 and she is usually said to have been 40; she supported him with her wealth; their children: al-Qasim, 'Abd Allah, Zaynab, Ruqayya, Umm Kulthum and Fatima; the sons died young; he did not marry another wife while she lived; she was first to believe in his prophethood. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What can Muslims learn from this marriage about choosing a partner? Explain.
parts.answer: Character and faithfulness matter more than wealth or age; a woman may propose; mutual respect and support build a strong marriage.
parts.working: Points may include: Khadija chose him for honesty, not wealth; he married an older, previously married woman; women's right to choose; mutual support in difficulty; respect for a wife's work and business. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Prophet's (pbuh) journey to Syria with Abu Talib when he was about twelve, including the meeting with the monk Bahira.
parts.answer: Abu Talib took him with a trading caravan to Syria; at Busra the Christian monk Bahira invited the travellers, observed the boy closely, recognised signs of a future prophet mentioned in his books and warned Abu Talib to take him home and protect him.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: aged about 9–12; Abu Talib could not bear to leave him; the caravan stopped at Busra in Syria; Bahira normally ignored caravans but invited them; he noticed a cloud shading the boy / a tree bending; questioned him and saw a mark between his shoulders (seal of prophethood); said he would be a prophet; advised Abu Talib to protect him from enemies; Abu Talib sent/took him back to Makka.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why do you think Muslims value accounts such as this from before the prophethood? Explain.
parts.answer: They show that people of earlier scriptures expected a prophet and that the Prophet (pbuh) was recognised and protected from childhood, strengthening belief in his mission.
parts.working: Points may include: links to earlier scriptures predicting a prophet; God's care for him from childhood; respect for honest people of other faiths; inspires faith; but Muslims rely mainly on the Qur'an, and such reports are supporting evidence. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how Zayd ibn Haritha and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib came to live in the household of the Prophet (pbuh) before prophethood.
parts.answer: Zayd had been captured as a child and sold as a slave; Khadija gave him to the Prophet (pbuh); when his father came to buy him back Zayd chose to stay, and the Prophet freed him and adopted him; 'Ali was taken into the Prophet's home as a young child to ease the burden on Abu Talib, who had many children and little money, during a hard time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: Zayd taken in a raid and sold in Makka; bought by Khadija's relative and given to her; she gave him to the Prophet (pbuh); his father and uncle came to ransom him; he was given the choice and chose to stay; the Prophet (pbuh) freed him and declared him his son at the Ka'ba; during a drought Abu Talib was struggling; the Prophet (pbuh) took 'Ali and al-'Abbas took Ja'far; 'Ali grew up in his house; both were among the first believers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Zayd chose the Prophet (pbuh) over his own family. Explain what this shows about the Prophet's (pbuh) character before prophethood.
parts.answer: He treated a servant with such kindness and respect that the boy preferred him to freedom with his family, showing his gentleness, fairness and love even before revelation.
parts.working: Points may include: kindness to servants and slaves; no harshness; made Zayd feel like family; generosity in freeing him; example for treatment of domestic workers today. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the life and character of the Prophet (pbuh) between the ages of twelve and forty, before prophethood.
parts.answer: At about twelve he went with Abu Talib on a trade journey to Syria, where the monk Bahira saw signs of prophethood in him; he worked as a shepherd and then as a trader; he joined the Hilf al-Fudul, a pact to protect the oppressed; he was known as al-Amin (the trustworthy) and al-Sadiq (the truthful); he traded for Khadija, who was impressed by his honesty and proposed marriage — he married her at 25; at about 35 he settled the dispute over replacing the Black Stone by placing it on a cloak that each clan leader lifted; he avoided idol worship and often retreated to the cave of Hira to reflect.
parts.working: Indicative content: Trade journey to Syria at about twelve; monk Bahira; shepherd; trader; Hilf al-Fudul; titles al-Amin / al-Sadiq; employed by Khadija; her servant Maysara reported his honesty; marriage at 25; rebuilding of the Ka'ba and the Black Stone dispute at 35; solution with the cloak; never worshipped idols; retreats to Hira. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Prophet's (pbuh) good character before prophethood was important for his later mission.
parts.answer: Because people already trusted him, it was harder for them to call him a liar, and his reputation gave weight to his message.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Point, development (e.g. the Quraysh admitted at Mount Safa that he had never lied). Model answer: Because people already trusted him, it was harder for them to call him a liar, and his reputation gave weight to his message. Marked by levels out of 4. Level 4 (4): a well-developed, reasoned answer (two developed points, or one fully developed point) linked to life today, with a clear judgement where the question asks for one. Level 3 (3): a reasoned answer with some development and a relevant example, but the judgement or link to today is less clear. Level 2 (2): one or two simple points with little development. Level 1 (1): a basic, general statement. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the religious and social conditions in Arabia before the coming of Islam (the jahiliyya).
parts.answer: Most Arabs worshipped idols, about 360 around the Ka'ba, alongside a vague belief in Allah; a few hanifs kept Ibrahim's faith; there were some Jews and Christians; society was tribal with constant feuds; drinking, gambling and usury were common; some buried baby daughters alive; women, slaves and orphans had few rights; but Arabs valued hospitality, courage and poetry.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): idols such as Hubal, al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat; the Ka'ba surrounded by idols; belief in Allah as a high god without proper worship; superstition, soothsayers, divining arrows; hanifs like Zayd ibn 'Amr rejected idols; Jewish tribes in Yathrib and Khaybar, Christians in Najran and among some tribes; loyalty to the tribe above justice; long blood feuds (e.g. Aws and Khazraj, Harb al-Fijar); raiding; alcohol, gambling; heavy interest on loans; female infanticide (81.8–9 refers to the buried girl); women inherited as property and had no limit on marriages; slaves mistreated; virtues: hospitality, generosity, bravery, eloquence, keeping protection agreements. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The pre-Islamic Arabs had nothing of value.' How far do you agree? Give reasons.
parts.answer: Disagree in part: Islam abolished idolatry and injustice but kept and purified good traditions such as hospitality, courage, keeping promises and eloquence; the Prophet (pbuh) said he came to perfect good character.
parts.working: Points may include: virtues were real: hospitality, bravery, loyalty, poetry, Hilf al-Fudul; Islam reformed rather than erased (hajj purified, Ka'ba kept); vices were serious; balanced judgement for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about 'Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's (pbuh) grandfather, and his role in the Prophet's early life.
parts.answer: He was leader of the Banu Hashim and responsible for giving water to pilgrims; he re-dug the well of Zamzam; he faced Abraha in the Year of the Elephant; he named his grandson Muhammad, took him into his care after Amina's death, loved him dearly, and died when the boy was about eight, asking Abu Talib to look after him.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: a respected chief of the Quraysh; in charge of siqaya (water) for pilgrims; re-discovered and dug Zamzam; his vow to sacrifice a son and Abdullah's ransom with 100 camels (as reported); met Abraha about his camels; chose the name Muhammad; took the orphan after Amina's death at al-Abwa'; let him sit on his special place by the Ka'ba; died when the boy was about 8; entrusted him to Abu Talib.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some people say the Prophet's (pbuh) early life shows God's care for him through the people around him. Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Agree with evidence: although he lost his parents, he was protected by Halima, 'Abd al-Muttalib and Abu Talib in turn, as Sura 93 says God found him an orphan and sheltered him; but these people also chose freely to show love and duty.
parts.working: Points may include: Sura 93.6; chain of guardians; Abu Talib's later protection in Makka; human kindness also matters as an example for families; evaluation for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Prophet's (pbuh) habit of retreating to the cave of Hira in the years before the first revelation, and the hanif tradition of the time.
parts.answer: In his late thirties he spent days, especially in Ramadan, alone in the cave on Mount Nur, taking food with him, reflecting on God and creation and turning away from idol worship; a few Makkans called hanifs also rejected idols and sought the religion of Ibrahim.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: cave of Hira on Jabal al-Nur near Makka; he went for several nights at a time; Khadija prepared provisions; especially in Ramadan; he disliked idol worship and never worshipped idols; meditation on God and the condition of society; hanifs such as Zayd ibn 'Amr and Waraqa ibn Nawfal rejected idols; true dreams came before revelation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Spending time alone is necessary for spiritual growth.' Evaluate this statement in the light of the Prophet's (pbuh) life.
parts.answer: Times of reflection, like at Hira and later in i'tikaf, are valuable, but after revelation the Prophet (pbuh) lived among people and taught that serving and mixing with people patiently is better than withdrawal.
parts.working: Points may include: Hira prepared him; i'tikaf in Ramadan continues the practice; reflection away from phones and noise today; but Islam rejects monastic withdrawal; balance of private worship and public duty; justified conclusion for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the experiences of the Prophet's (pbuh) life before the age of forty prepared him for his mission.
parts.answer: Orphanhood gave him dependence on God and compassion for the weak; desert life gave eloquence and strength; shepherding taught patience; trade made him travel and understand people and gave him a reputation for honesty; the Pact of the Virtuous and the Black Stone arbitration showed justice and leadership; marriage to Khadija gave security and support; reflection at Hira prepared him spiritually.

parts.text: Describe the main themes of Sura 112 (al-Ikhlas).

parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: God is One (tawhid); He is unique / without partner; He is eternal / self-sufficient, the One all creatures turn to in need; He has no offspring; He was not born of anyone (has no beginning); nothing in creation is equal or similar to Him; the sura rejects ideas of God having a family. Do not credit background about the sura's name or place of revelation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a Muslim can show belief in the teaching of this sura in daily life.
parts.answer: By worshipping and relying on God alone, avoiding anything that gives His position to another, and treating all people as equal servants of the one God.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 per relevant action, +1 for developing it with a reason or example. Points may include: praying and making du'a to God alone, not to any created being; relying on God in difficulty rather than on luck or superstition; not letting money, status or people take first place in one's life; treating all people as equal because all are created by the one God; sincerity (doing good for God's pleasure, not show).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the themes of Sura 42.4–5.
parts.answer: Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God; He is the Most High, the Most Great; the heavens almost split apart from above out of awe of Him; the angels glorify Him and ask forgiveness for those on earth; He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: ownership of everything; Most High, Most Great; heavens almost break apart from His majesty; angels praise Him; angels pray for forgiveness for people on earth; God is the Forgiving, the Merciful.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The passage says the angels ask forgiveness for those on earth. Explain how this should affect a Muslim's attitude to repentance.
parts.answer: It shows that forgiveness is wanted for people even by the angels and that God is the Forgiving, the Merciful, so a Muslim should repent quickly and hopefully rather than despairing.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Encouragement to repent; hope rather than despair; God's mercy; praying for others' forgiveness too; example. Marked by levels out of 4. parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the themes of Sura 41.37.
parts.answer: Night and day, the sun and the moon are among God's signs; people should not bow down to the sun or the moon; they should bow down to God who created them; this is if they truly worship Him.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: night and day as signs; sun and moon as signs; command not to prostrate to sun or moon; prostrate to God, their Creator; worship belongs to God alone / creation points to the Creator.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this teaching applies to modern superstitions such as horoscopes and lucky charms.
parts.answer: Sun, moon and stars are signs created by God and have no power of their own, so believing that the stars decide one's future or that a charm brings luck gives creation a power that belongs to God.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Creation has no independent power; trust in God alone; horoscopes, charms, 'unlucky' days; link to 41.37; developed example. Marked by levels out of 4. parts.text: Ayat al-Kursi (Sura 2.255) says that neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes God and that guarding the heavens and the earth does not tire Him. Explain what these phrases teach about God.
parts.answer: God is the Ever-Living and the Self-Subsisting Sustainer of all; unlike created beings He has no weakness or need for rest; His care for and control over the whole universe never stops for a moment; nothing happens without His knowledge, and He is the Most High, the Most Great.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: Ever-Living (al-Hayy); Self-Subsisting/Sustainer (al-Qayyum); no weakness or need, unlike creation; constant, uninterrupted care and control; heavens and earth upheld without effort; Most High, Most Great.

parts.answer: When she is tired or alone at night, she knows God is awake and watching over her patients and her family; she can rely on Him, do her best and trust Him with what she cannot control.

parts.answer: God is the Originator of the heavens and earth; He cannot have a son as He has no partner; He created everything and knows everything; He alone deserves worship and takes care of all affairs; no vision can grasp Him but He sees all; He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The passage says that no human vision can grasp God. Explain how this teaching should affect the way Muslims think about God.
parts.answer: Muslims should not picture God as a created form or make images of Him; they understand Him through His names, attributes and signs, while knowing He sees them at all times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how 'Umar became caliph and the attitude he showed at the start of his caliphate.
parts.answer: During his final illness in 13 AH (634 CE) Abu Bakr consulted senior Companions such as 'Abdur Rahman bin 'Awf and 'Uthman about 'Umar; some worried about his strictness, but Abu Bakr said responsibility would soften him; he had his nomination written down by 'Uthman and read to the people, who accepted it and gave their pledge; 'Umar was known as al-Faruq and became the first to be called Amir al-Mu'minin; in his first address he said he would be gentle with the good and firm with wrongdoers, asked people to correct him and promised to serve them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the main administrative reforms introduced by 'Umar.
parts.answer: He divided the empire into provinces run by governors; appointed judges (qadis) separate from governors; organised the treasury (bayt al-mal); set up the diwan, a register for paying stipends to soldiers and citizens; introduced the Hijri calendar; built garrison towns such as Basra, Kufa and Fustat; organised a police and army system with regular pay; carried out land surveys and kept conquered land under state control for revenue; dug canals and built roads; set up guest houses and helped the poor and elderly.

parts.answer: It was fought in 11–12 AH against Musaylima, the false prophet, and the Banu Hanifa; the Muslim army under Khalid ibn al-Walid met a large force and suffered early setbacks; the enemy retreated into a walled garden, later called the Garden of Death, where fierce fighting took place; Musaylima was killed (Wahshi is reported to have struck him) and the Muslims won, but many Companions, including many memorisers of the Qur'an, were killed.

parts.answer: So many memorisers died that 'Umar feared parts of the Qur'an could be lost if more battles followed, so he urged Abu Bakr to have it collected in one written copy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Qur'an was compiled during the caliphate of Abu Bakr.
parts.answer: After Yamama 'Umar urged Abu Bakr to collect the Qur'an; Abu Bakr hesitated because the Prophet (pbuh) had not done it, but became convinced; he chose Zayd ibn Thabit, a young, trusted scribe who had been present at the Prophet's last review of the Qur'an; Zayd also hesitated, then began; he collected verses from written materials (palm stalks, stones, leather) and from people who had memorised them; he accepted written material only when it was confirmed – reportedly by two witnesses that it had been written in the Prophet's presence; the last verses of Sura 9 were found with only one Companion; the collected sheets (suhuf) were kept by Abu Bakr, then 'Umar, then Hafsa.

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that every action is valued according to the intention behind it, and each person receives the result of what they truly meant to do.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Deeds are judged by the intention in the heart; God rewards sincerity, so the same outward act can be worthy or worthless depending on its purpose; a believer's actions should be done for God's pleasure.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: intention (niyya) is the basis of every deed; God knows what is in the heart; reward depends on sincerity, not outward appearance; good acts done for show or worldly gain lose their reward; ordinary acts can become worship with a good intention; each person is responsible for their own intention.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Muslims can put this teaching into practice in their daily lives.
parts.answer: By renewing a sincere intention before actions — study, work, charity, worship — so that they are done for God rather than praise, and by checking their motives.

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) said that whoever does not thank people has not thanked God.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Thanking people who help us is part of thanking God; ingratitude to people shows a lack of gratitude to God; God often sends His blessings through other people.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: thanking people is required; link between thanking people and thanking God; God's blessings come through people; ingratitude is a fault of faith.

parts.label: b

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): When asked about the highest level of faith, the Prophet (pbuh) explained that it is to worship God as though you can see Him, and although you cannot see Him, to know that He certainly sees you.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith about ihsan (excellence in faith).
parts.answer: Ihsan is the highest level of faith: worshipping with full awareness of God's presence, as if seeing Him; since He sees everything, the believer acts sincerely and carefully in public and private.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: ihsan is the highest stage of religion (after islam and iman); worship with complete focus and devotion; awareness that God is always watching; this produces sincerity and humility; excellence in all actions, not only prayer; part of the well-known Hadith in which Jibril questioned the Prophet (pbuh).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this teaching can improve a Muslim's prayer and behaviour.
parts.answer: Awareness of God's presence brings concentration and humility in prayer, and makes the believer honest and careful even when no one else is watching.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: focus and calm in salat, avoiding rushing or distraction by the phone (1+1); honesty in private, e.g. not cheating in an online test (1); doing work to the best standard because God sees it (1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): A man asked the Prophet (pbuh) whether he should leave his camel untied and trust in God, or tie it and trust in God. The Prophet (pbuh) told him to tie it and then trust in God.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Trust in God (tawakkul) does not mean doing nothing; a Muslim must take sensible practical steps and then rely on God for the result.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: tawakkul is part of faith; it must be combined with effort; people must take reasonable precautions; the result is in God's hands; laziness is not trust; balance between action and reliance on God.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of how a Muslim can act on this Hadith today, explaining each.
parts.answer: E.g. a student revises thoroughly and then prays for success, accepting the result; a family in a flood-prone area in Sindh prepares and follows warnings while trusting God; a traveller locks the car and trusts God.
parts.working: 2 marks per example: 1 for the action (effort / precaution), 1 for explaining how trust in God is added (prayer, calm acceptance of outcome).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that none of you truly has faith until he wants for his brother what he wants for himself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Complete faith includes caring for others; a believer should wish good for others as for himself, avoid jealousy and selfishness, and see other believers as brothers and sisters.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: faith is not complete without love for others; wish the same good for others as for yourself; removes envy and selfishness; brotherhood / sisterhood among believers; many scholars extend this to all humanity; faith shown in attitudes and conduct towards others.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can Muslims show this teaching in action? Give examples.
parts.answer: By sharing, helping others succeed, being happy at their success and treating others as they would like to be treated.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed examples, e.g.: sharing notes with a classmate before exams instead of hiding them (1+1); congratulating a colleague's promotion without envy (1); giving good-quality items in charity, the kind one would want oneself (1+1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that whoever believes in God and the Last Day should either say something good or remain silent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what this Hadith teaches about the link between belief and speech.
parts.answer: Belief in God and the Day of Judgement should show in how a Muslim speaks; since words are recorded and will be judged, the believer speaks only what is good and otherwise stays silent.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: true faith affects behaviour; speech is an important part of conduct; belief in the Last Day — words will be accounted for; say only what is good, true and useful; avoid lies, backbiting, insults, gossip; silence is better than harmful speech.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can Muslims apply this teaching to their use of social media?
parts.answer: By posting and commenting only what is true and beneficial, not spreading rumours or insulting people, and staying silent rather than joining arguments or gossip.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: checking facts before sharing (1+1); avoiding hurtful comments, mockery or backbiting online (1); using platforms to spread useful knowledge or kindness (1); stepping away from heated arguments (1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) said that the affair of the believer is wonderful, for all of it is good: if something good happens to him he is thankful, and that is good for him; if something harmful happens he is patient, and that is good for him. This is only for the believer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what this Hadith teaches about the believer's attitude to good times and bad times.
parts.answer: A believer is grateful to God when good comes and patient when harm comes; both responses earn reward, so every situation is good for the believer; faith changes how events are experienced.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: gratitude in ease; patience in hardship; both bring reward; every situation is good for the true believer; this applies only to the believer (faith is the key).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this teaching could help a family in Pakistan whose business has suffered losses.
parts.answer: They remain patient, avoid despair or blame, keep praying and working to recover, and stay thankful for health and family, trusting the loss carries reward.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Patience; avoiding despair; continuing effort; gratitude for remaining blessings; link to reward. Marked by levels out of 4. practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) took hold of a Companion's shoulder and told him to be in this world as though he were a stranger or a traveller passing along a road.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: A Muslim should not become too attached to this world, which is temporary like a journey; a traveller takes only what he needs and keeps his destination in mind, so the believer focuses on the Hereafter while living responsibly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: world is temporary; detachment from worldly attachment; stranger/traveller image – not settling; focus on the Hereafter; this does not mean abandoning duties.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Does this Hadith mean Muslims should not try to succeed in their careers? Give reasons.

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) said that no one with even a tiny amount of pride in his heart will enter Paradise. A man asked about liking good clothes and shoes. The Prophet (pbuh) replied that God is beautiful and loves beauty; pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what this Hadith teaches about pride.
parts.answer: Pride is not about liking good things such as clean clothes; God is beautiful and loves beauty; pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people; even a tiny amount of pride is very serious.

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that God divided mercy into one hundred parts; He kept ninety-nine with Himself and sent down one part to the earth, and it is from that one part that all creatures show mercy to one another, even an animal lifting its hoof so as not to harm its young.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what this Hadith teaches about God's mercy.
parts.answer: God's mercy is immense, far greater than all the mercy found in creation; every act of kindness on earth comes from a small portion of it; He keeps the greater share for His servants in the Hereafter, which gives hope of forgiveness.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: mercy is one of God's greatest attributes; all compassion in creation comes from Him; the mercy seen on earth is only a tiny share; ninety-nine parts are kept for the Day of Judgement; even animals' care for their young is from God's mercy; believers should never despair of God's mercy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Knowing that God is so merciful may make people careless about sin.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: Disagree mostly: God's mercy should lead to gratitude, hope and repentance rather than carelessness; Muslims balance hope in mercy with fear of accountability, and mercy also calls them to be merciful to others.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: a clear judgement (1); mercy brings hope and encourages repentance, not complacency (1); balance of hope and fear / accountability on the Day of Judgement (1); believers are expected to reflect this mercy to others, with example (1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) said that a hypocrite has three signs: when he speaks he lies, when he makes a promise he breaks it, and when he is trusted he betrays the trust.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what this Hadith teaches about the qualities expected of a true believer.
parts.answer: A believer's faith must be matched by honesty, keeping promises and faithfulness to trusts; lying, breaking promises and betraying trust are signs of hypocrisy, where outward faith hides an inner fault.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: faith must be shown in character; truthfulness is essential; promises must be kept; trusts (amanah) must be honoured, including property, secrets and responsibilities; these three faults are signs of hypocrisy (nifaq); a believer should examine himself for them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: To what extent is keeping promises the most important of these three qualities in modern society? Give reasons.
parts.answer: A reasoned judgement, e.g. all three are linked — business contracts, family commitments and public office all depend on promises, but honesty underlies keeping promises and trusts, so truthfulness may be the foundation.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: judgement (1); reasoned support for promises, e.g. contracts, deadlines, marriage (1); comparison with truthfulness or trust, e.g. public officials handling funds (1); modern example and conclusion (1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that this world is like a prison for the believer and like a paradise for the disbeliever.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: The believer restrains desires and follows God's limits in this life, so it feels restricting compared with the reward awaiting him; the disbeliever treats this world as his only enjoyment, and it is the best he will have compared with what follows; this life is temporary and a test.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: this world is temporary; it is a test; the believer accepts limits set by God (lawful and unlawful); the believer's true home and reward are in the Hereafter; compared with Paradise, worldly life is restricted; for one who rejects the Hereafter, worldly pleasure is all there is; it does not mean believers must be unhappy or reject lawful enjoyment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this teaching can help Muslims cope with hardship and temptation.
parts.answer: It reminds them that difficulties and self-restraint are temporary and will be rewarded, so they stay patient in hardship and resist temptations that bring short pleasure but long regret.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: patience in illness, poverty or loss knowing it is temporary (1+1); resisting unlawful income or pleasures by keeping the Hereafter in mind (1+1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) said that religion is sincerity (sincere goodwill). The Companions asked, 'To whom?' He said: to God, to His Book, to His Messenger, to the leaders of the Muslims and to their common people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what this Hadith teaches about the meaning of religion.

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that what is lawful is clear and what is unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters which many people do not know. practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that the strong person is not the one who defeats others in wrestling; the strong person is the one who controls himself when he is angry.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Real strength is self-control, not physical power; a Muslim should control anger and not act on it through violence or harsh words.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: true strength is moral / inner strength; physical strength is not the measure of a person; anger must be controlled; acting in anger leads to harm and regret; self-discipline is a sign of faith; patience is praised in Islam.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain practical ways a Muslim can act on this Hadith.
parts.answer: By staying calm in arguments, keeping quiet, changing position, making wudu, seeking refuge in God from Satan and forgiving others.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 per method, +1 for development, e.g.: staying silent or walking away during a quarrel (1+1); sitting down if standing, making wudu (1); seeking refuge in God (1); calm driving in Karachi traffic instead of road rage (1+1); forgiving instead of taking revenge (1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that whoever among you sees something wrong should change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; and if he cannot, then in his heart, and that is the weakest level of faith.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Muslims have a duty to oppose wrong in the way they are able: by action if they have the authority, by speaking out if not, and at least by hating it in the heart; it is part of faith to care about wrongdoing in society.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: duty to forbid wrong; three levels — action, speech, heart; according to one's ability and authority; changing by hand means proper action by those responsible, not violence by individuals; disliking wrong in the heart is the minimum; faith is linked to social responsibility.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of how a Muslim today can act on this Hadith at different levels.
parts.answer: E.g. a teacher stops bullying in her class (hand); a student speaks up politely when friends mock someone (tongue); a person who cannot act stays away from a gathering where backbiting takes place and prays for change (heart).
parts.working: 2 marks per example: 1 for a suitable wrong and action, 1 for linking it to the correct level and to the person's ability.

parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Charity is not only giving money; simple kind acts such as a smile are rewarded; Muslims should be cheerful and friendly, spreading happiness and brotherhood.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: charity (sadaqa) has many forms; even small acts are rewarded; a smile spreads love and goodwill; it costs nothing, so everyone can give; good manners are part of faith; strengthens brotherhood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Muslims can act on this teaching in a busy city such as Karachi or New York.
parts.answer: By greeting neighbours, shopkeepers and colleagues warmly, welcoming newcomers at the mosque and being cheerful with family, which builds friendship in places where people often feel isolated.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed examples: greeting and smiling at colleagues and staff (1+1); welcoming new students or neighbours (1); positive manner with family after a stressful day (1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for those in his care: the ruler for his people, a man for his family, a woman for her husband's home and children, and a servant for his master's property.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Everyone has responsibilities over others or over trusts given to them, and will be asked about how they carried them out; this applies to rulers, parents, spouses and workers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: everyone is a guardian / shepherd; responsibility is a trust (amanah); rulers responsible for citizens; husbands for families; wives for the home and children; employees for property in their care; all will be questioned by God; no one is without responsibility.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this Hadith can guide two different people in Pakistan today, such as a government official and a parent.
parts.answer: The official must serve citizens honestly, avoid corruption and use public funds properly; the parent must provide, educate and give a good example to children, knowing both will be asked by God.
parts.working: 2 marks per person: 1 for a relevant responsibility, 1 for development (e.g. official — fair service, no bribes; parent — religious and academic education, time and love).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that God is gentle and loves gentleness in every matter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Gentleness is one of God's qualities and He loves it in people; Muslims should be kind and soft in manner in all situations, avoiding harshness, which spoils things.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: gentleness (rifq) is loved by God; it applies to all matters; harshness is disliked; gentleness achieves what harshness cannot; it is part of good character; the Prophet (pbuh) himself was gentle with people.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Muslims can show gentleness in family life and at work.
parts.answer: By speaking softly to children and elderly parents, correcting mistakes kindly, being patient with colleagues and customers and treating animals with care.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed examples: correcting a child's mistake calmly rather than shouting (1+1); patience with ageing parents (1); a manager giving feedback respectfully (1); kindness to animals (1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) instructed that a worker should be given his wages before his sweat has dried.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Employers must pay workers fully and promptly; delaying wages is injustice; workers' rights and dignity must be respected; fair dealing is part of faith.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: pay wages promptly; pay the full agreed amount; delay or cheating is oppression; respect the dignity of labour; workers depend on wages for their families; fairness in business is required by Islam.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can this Hadith be put into practice by employers today?
parts.answer: By paying salaries on time, honouring agreed wages, giving fair pay to domestic workers and daily-wage labourers, and providing safe working conditions.

practice.subtopic: The Hadiths and other sources of Islamic law

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Hadiths are the second source of Islamic law after the Qur'an, referring to what the Qur'an says about the Prophet (pbuh).
parts.answer: The Qur'an commands believers to obey God and obey the Messenger (e.g. Sura 4.59); it tells them to take whatever the Messenger gives and avoid what he forbids (Sura 59.7); it calls him an excellent example to follow (Sura 33.21); it says he does not speak from his own desire but from revelation (Sura 53.3–4); his role was to explain the Qur'an, so his words and actions are needed to practise it; but the Hadiths come second because they are reported by people and must agree with the Qur'an, which is God's own word.

practice.subtopic: The Hadiths and other sources of Islamic law

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Sunna includes the sayings, actions and silent approval of the Prophet (pbuh). Explain each of these, giving an example.
parts.answer: Sayings: his words teaching or commanding, e.g. his teaching that actions are judged by intentions. Actions: what he did, which Companions observed and copied, e.g. how he performed prayer, wudu and hajj. Silent approval: something done in his presence or known to him which he did not object to, showing it is allowed, e.g. Companions eating a desert lizard in front of him although he himself did not eat it.
parts.working: Indicative content: Sayings (qawl) — his words, e.g. 'actions are judged by intentions'; actions (fi'l) — what he did, e.g. how he prayed or performed hajj ('pray as you have seen me pray'); silent approval (taqrir) — what was done in his presence that he did not forbid, e.g. eating the lizard (dabb), or the Companions' different times for 'Asr on the way to Banu Qurayza. All three types, each explained with an example, are needed for Level 4. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why is the Prophet's silent approval an important source of law?
parts.answer: He would not stay silent about something wrong, as his task was to guide; so his silence shows that the practice is permitted, which gives Muslims a wider range of lawful actions and shows Islam's ease.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: He would correct wrong; silence = permission / ease. practice.subtopic: The Hadiths and other sources of Islamic law

parts.text: Explain the terms ahl al-hadith and ahl al-ra'y as used in early Islamic scholarship.
parts.answer: Ahl al-hadith were scholars who relied heavily on the reports of the Prophet (pbuh) and the Companions and were cautious about personal reasoning. Ahl al-ra'y used reasoned judgement and analogy more widely, especially where few reports were available. Both took the Qur'an as the basis of law.

parts.answer: Both gave weight to the Qur'an and the Sunna. Over time the two approaches influenced each other, and later scholars used Hadith and reasoned methods together, for example through analogy based on the sources.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the isnad and the matn of a Hadith.
parts.answer: The isnad is the chain of narrators through whom the Hadith has been passed down, from the collector back to the Prophet (pbuh), e.g. 'A told me that B told him that C heard the Prophet say…'. The matn is the actual text or content of the Hadith, what the Prophet (pbuh) said, did or approved.

parts.answer: (i) Abu Hurayra. Hasan (good): meets the same conditions but one or more narrators has a slightly weaker memory; accepted and used for law. parts.answer: A Hadith that looks sound on the surface but has a hidden fault in its chain or text, which only experts can detect. For example, a narrator may have been confused, or a chain may have been connected wrongly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: the report appears sound; it has a hidden fault in the chain or text; only experts can find it; an example such as a confused narrator or a wrongly connected chain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how Hadith scholars detect such a hidden defect.
parts.answer: By comparing many narrations of the same Hadith from different routes, checking the memory and records of the narrators, noticing contradictions between versions, and examining the details of the text.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: comparing different routes of the same report; checking the memory and records of narrators; noticing contradictions between versions; examining the text for unusual details. Maximum 4.

practice.subtopic: Isnad, matn and classification of Hadiths

parts.label: a
parts.text: Was the isnad (chain of narrators) more important than the matn (text) in deciding whether a Hadith was accepted? Give reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: A balanced answer that takes a position. The isnad was central to early scholars because it showed whether the report could be trusted. However, the matn was also examined, for agreement with the Qur'an, with other sound Hadiths, with reason and with known facts. A Hadith with a strong chain could be rejected if its text was contrary to these tests, so both were needed for a sound judgement.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): the isnad showed the reliability of narrators; scholars studied the honesty, memory and continuity of narrators; the matn was checked against the Qur'an and sound Hadiths; a text that was illogical or contrary to known facts could lead to rejection; a Hadith with a sound chain can still have a weak or hidden defect; both are needed for judgement; a clear position supported by reasons. Levels: 9–10 a balanced, well-argued answer with a clear judgement and several accurate points; 6–8 a good answer with some judgement; 3–5 a basic outline; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Hadiths were preserved during the lifetime of the Prophet (pbuh) and the time of the Companions.
parts.answer: Companions memorised his words and observed his actions, often learning in groups and repeating them; at first he discouraged writing Hadiths in case they were confused with the Qur'an, but later some Companions were allowed to write, e.g. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, whose notebook was called al-Sahifa al-Sadiqa; his letters and treaties were kept in writing; after his death Companions such as Abu Hurayra, 'A'isha, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Anas ibn Malik taught many students; they were careful and checked each other's reports; Companions spread to new cities and taught there.
parts.working: Indicative content: Memorisation; practice/observing; early discouragement of writing (reason); later permission; 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr's al-Sahifa al-Sadiqa; written letters/treaties; named Companions who narrated many Hadiths; teaching students; caution/checking; spread to new cities. Marked by levels out of 10. parts.label: b
parts.text: Why did the Prophet (pbuh) at first discourage writing his sayings?
parts.answer: So that his words would not be mixed up with the Qur'an while it was still being revealed and written; once the Qur'an was well known and distinct, writing was allowed.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Fear of confusion with the Qur'an; later allowed when the risk had passed. parts.label: a
parts.text: State the compiler of Sahih Muslim.
parts.answer: Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the two collections that are generally regarded as the most authentic (sahih) collections in Sunni Hadith literature.
parts.answer: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the two correct collections.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three of the Six Books whose titles begin with the word 'Sunan'.
parts.answer: Sunan Abi Dawud; Sunan al-Nasa'i; Sunan Ibn Majah.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three correct titles. Maximum 3.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As; al-Sahifa al-Sadiqa (the truthful page).
parts.working: 1 mark for the Companion; 1 mark for the title.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the reason the Prophet (pbuh) gave for allowing him to write down what he heard, according to this Companion's report.
parts.answer: The Prophet (pbuh) said that he says nothing but the truth.
parts.working: 1 mark for permission being given; 1 mark for the reason, that the Prophet (pbuh) says only the truth.

parts.answer: Imam al-Tirmidhi (Abu 'Isa Muhammad ibn 'Isa); Ibn Majah (Muhammad ibn Yazid).

parts.label: a

parts.answer: Imam Malik ibn Anas; Madina.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how al-Muwatta' is arranged.
parts.answer: It is arranged by legal topics. It includes Hadiths together with the practice and opinions of Companions and Successors.
parts.working: 1 mark for arrangement by legal subject; 1 mark for including the practice and opinions of Companions and Successors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the stage of Hadith collection in the time of the Successors (Tabi'un), including the role of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz.
parts.answer: As the Companions died and fabrication grew, the need for written collection increased; the Umayyad caliph 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz ordered scholars and governors to collect and write down the Hadiths so that they would not be lost; Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri was among the first to collect them on this order; scholars travelled across the Muslim lands to gather reports; collections were often arranged by topic and mixed with sayings of Companions and rulings; Imam Malik's al-Muwatta' in Madina is an early surviving example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a musnad and a musannaf collection of Hadiths, and give an example of each.
parts.answer: Musnad: Hadiths arranged by the name of the Companion who narrated them, all reports of one Companion together, e.g. the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Musannaf: Hadiths arranged by subject (e.g. purification, prayer, zakat, trade), e.g. the Sahih of al-Bukhari or the Sahih of Muslim.
parts.working: 1 mark: musnad definition; 1 mark: musnad example; 1 mark: musannaf definition; 1 mark: musannaf example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which type of collection would be more useful to a judge needing a ruling on a business contract, and which to a scholar studying the reports of 'A'isha? Explain your answers.
parts.answer: The judge would use a musannaf, because all Hadiths on trade and contracts are found together under one chapter; the scholar would use a musnad, because all the reports narrated by 'A'isha are grouped under her name, making it easy to study her narrations and check them.
parts.working: 2 marks each: correct type (1) and reason (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih.
parts.answer: A short early collection of Hadiths written down by Hammam ibn Munabbih, a student who had learned from the Companion Abu Hurayra.
parts.working: 1 mark for an early written collection; 1 mark for Hammam ibn Munabbih as the compiler; 1 mark for learning from Abu Hurayra.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why such early written collections are important for studying the history of the Hadiths.
parts.answer: They show that Hadiths were recorded in writing early, so the text can be compared with later collections. They also help scholars check the chains and how reports were passed on.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: early writing shows the Hadiths were recorded early; the text can be compared with later books; chains can be checked; the transmission can be traced; it supports the study of authenticity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what Imam al-Tirmidhi did for many of the Hadiths in his Jami' that is useful to readers.
parts.answer: He graded many Hadiths (for example as sahih, hasan or gharib) and explained the views of scholars on their ruling.
parts.working: 1 mark for grading the Hadiths; 1 mark for explaining scholars' views.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the term hasan (fair or good) in Hadith classification.
parts.answer: A Hadith whose narrators are reliable but slightly less exact in memory than those of a sahih Hadith. It can still be used as evidence.
parts.working: 1 mark for reliable narrators with slightly less exact memory than a sahih Hadith; 1 mark for it being usable as evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim are called sahih, while Sunan Abi Dawud includes some weaker reports as well.
parts.answer: The Sahih collections set out to include only reports that are authentic in their main chapters. Sunan Abi Dawud collected Hadiths about law, and Abu Dawud noted weaker reports and his own judgement of them so that readers could weigh them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: the Sahih collections aim at authentic reports; they keep the main chapters to authentic reports; Abu Dawud's Sunan gathered legal Hadiths; weaker reports were included and noted; readers can judge the grading. Maximum 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Imam al-Bukhari was born in 194 AH and died in 256 AH. Calculate his age at death in lunar years.
parts.answer: 62 lunar years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the century AH in which he died.
parts.answer: The 3rd century AH.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what a jami' collection of Hadith is.
parts.answer: A collection arranged by topics, covering many subjects such as belief, worship, dealings, manners and history. Sahih al-Bukhari and Jami' al-Tirmidhi are examples.
parts.working: 1 mark for arrangement by topics; 1 mark for naming two or more subject areas; 1 mark for a correct example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the 'golden age' of Hadith compilation in the third century after the migration, naming the main collections.
parts.answer: In the third century AH (ninth century CE) scholars produced the most respected collections, using strict methods to check chains and texts; the six main Sunni collections are the Sahih of al-Bukhari, the Sahih of Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, and the Sunan of Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah; al-Bukhari and Muslim included only Hadiths they judged sahih; the Sunan works focused on legal Hadiths and noted the strength of reports; the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal is also from this time. Shi'a Muslims rely mainly on four later collections: al-Kafi (al-Kulayni), Man la yahduruhu al-faqih (al-Saduq), and Tahdhib al-ahkam and al-Istibsar (al-Tusi).

parts.text: Why do you think the third century was the right time for these great collections to be made?
parts.answer: By then Hadiths were spread in many cities and could be gathered by travel; the science of narrators had developed fully; fabrication had become widespread, so a reliable selection was urgently needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about Imam al-Bukhari and the method he used in compiling his Sahih.
parts.answer: He was born in Bukhara in Central Asia in 810 CE; he showed a remarkable memory from childhood; he travelled widely (Makka, Madina, Iraq, Syria, Egypt) to learn from hundreds of teachers; he is said to have collected hundreds of thousands of reports and selected only about seven thousand (including repeats) for his Sahih over about sixteen years; he accepted a Hadith only if each narrator was reliable and was known to have actually met the one he narrated from; it is reported that he made ablution and prayed before recording each Hadith; he arranged the book by subject; it is regarded by Sunni Muslims as the most authentic book after the Qur'an; he died in 870 CE near Samarqand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a musnad and a musannaf collection, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: A musnad arranges Hadiths under the Companion who narrated them, for example Musnad Ahmad ibn Hanbal. A musannaf arranges Hadiths by legal and other topics, for example the Musannaf of 'Abd al-Razzaq.
