parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between a sunan and a mu'jam collection, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: A sunan arranges Hadiths by legal topics, such as worship and transactions, for example Sunan Abi Dawud. A mu'jam arranges Hadiths by the teachers (shaykhs) from whom the compiler heard them, for example the Mu'jam of al-Tabarani.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: sunan arranged by legal subject; example of a sunan; mu'jam arranged by teachers; example of a mu'jam.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one major Shi'i collection of Hadiths and its compiler.
parts.answer: Al-Kafi, compiled by Muhammad ibn Ya'qub al-Kulayni.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both Sunni and Shi'i scholars studied the Sunna, and what this shows about the Hadiths as a shared source.
parts.answer: Both use the Qur'an and the Sunna as foundations of Islamic law and belief. Both preserved and examined reports through chains of narrators and the texts themselves. Both show reverence for the Prophet (pbuh). They differ on which narrators and sources they accept.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: both use the Qur'an and Sunna as foundations; both preserved reports; both examined chains and texts; shared reverence for the Prophet (pbuh); differences in the narrators and sources they accept. Maximum 4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one difference in what Shi'i and Sunni collections emphasise.
parts.answer: Shi'i collections give great weight to reports from the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, which Sunni collections do not treat in the same way.
parts.working: 1 mark for reports from the Imams being included; 1 mark for a difference in emphasis or in acceptance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assess the claim that Sahih al-Bukhari is the most reliable book after the Qur'an.
parts.answer: A balanced judgement. In favour: the book's strict aims and conditions, Imam al-Bukhari's careful travelling and checking, and the high esteem given to it by many later scholars. Against or with caution: reliability is judged by each Hadith rather than by the book as a whole, and scholars rank the books differently.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): the strict conditions and aims of Bukhari; his journeys and checking of narrators; the praise of later scholars; the Muslim scholars' ranking differs; a Hadith in any book is judged on its own chain and text; a balanced conclusion with reasons. Levels: 9–10 a balanced, well-argued judgement with several accurate points; 6–8 a good answer with some judgement; 3–5 a basic outline; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about how Imam al-Tirmidhi's grading and notes help readers judge the reliability of Hadiths and understand the views of different scholars.
parts.answer: Al-Tirmidhi graded many Hadiths and noted the views of scholars on them, so a reader can see both the ruling and the reasons. His notes show the legal views of different scholars and the points of weakness in a report, which helps students weigh the evidence.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: grading of Hadiths; a judgement on the reliability of a report; notes on scholars' views; notes on the weakness of a narrator or chain; help to understand legal differences; a guide for students to weigh evidence. Maximum 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Was the written collection of Hadiths in the first two centuries after the Hijra the most important development in preserving the Sunna? Give reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: A balanced answer that takes a position. Written collections gave a lasting, organised record of the Sunna, so Muslims were no longer dependent on memory alone. However, memorisation, oral teaching, the scholars' method of checking chains and texts, and the work of the Companions and Successors were also essential to preserving the Sunna.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): written collections gave an organised, lasting record; they made checking and teaching easier; memory and oral teaching remained important; the chain-checking method was essential; the work of Companions and Successors came before the written books; a clear judgement. Levels: 9–10 a balanced, well-argued judgement with several accurate points; 6–8 a good account with some judgement; 3–5 a basic outline; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which writing down the Hadiths changed the way Muslims learned the Sunna.
parts.answer: Learners could consult organised books instead of relying only on memory. Teachers could use the collections in classes, and the texts could be checked against each other.
parts.working: 2 marks for each of two ways with an explanation, for example: learners could consult organised books; teachers could use the collections in lessons; texts could be compared and checked; the collections gave a permanent record.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about Abu Bakr's support for the Prophet (pbuh) during the Makkan period and the migration to Madina.
parts.answer: He was a close friend and the first free adult man to accept Islam; he brought others to Islam, such as 'Uthman, al-Zubayr, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Talha; he spent his wealth freeing persecuted slaves including Bilal; he confirmed the Night Journey at once when others mocked, earning the title al-Siddiq; he was chosen to accompany the Prophet (pbuh) on the migration and prepared camels; they hid in the cave of Thawr for three nights, where the Qur'an calls him 'the second of two' (Sura 9.40); his family helped (his daughter Asma brought food, his son 'Abdullah brought news).

parts.text: Describe how 'Umar ibn al-Khattab accepted Islam.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the life of Bilal ibn Rabah.
parts.answer: He was an Abyssinian slave of Umayya ibn Khalaf in Makka; he accepted Islam early; his master tortured him, laying him on burning sand with a heavy rock on his chest; he kept repeating 'One, One' (God is One); Abu Bakr bought and freed him; he migrated to Madina; he was chosen as the first caller to prayer (mu'adhdhin) because of his fine voice; he fought at Badr and other battles; at the conquest of Makka he called the adhan from the top of the Ka'ba; after the Prophet's death he went to Syria.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: Fajr: from dawn until sunrise; Zuhr: just after midday when the sun passes its highest point; 'Asr: in the afternoon; Maghrib: just after sunset; 'Isha: at night, after twilight has gone.

parts.label: a

parts.answer: During the Night Journey and Ascension (al-Isra' wa al-Mi'raj) the Prophet (pbuh) was taken to the heavens; God made prayers obligatory there, first a larger number; on Musa's advice the Prophet (pbuh) asked for a reduction several times until it became five, with the reward of fifty.

parts.text: Describe the call to prayer (adhan) and its importance in the Muslim community.
parts.answer: It is called aloud by the mu'adhdhin before each obligatory prayer; it declares that God is the Greatest, bears witness that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His Messenger, calls people to come to prayer and to success, and ends by declaring God's greatness and oneness; Bilal was the first mu'adhdhin in Madina; it announces the time of prayer to the community, gathers people to the mosque, publicly declares the message of Islam, and is also whispered into the ear of a newborn baby.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the concessions Islam allows in prayer for a traveller and for a person who is ill.
parts.answer: A traveller on a journey of the required distance may shorten the four-unit prayers (Zuhr, 'Asr, 'Isha) to two units, while Fajr and Maghrib stay the same; travellers may also combine prayers (Zuhr with 'Asr and Maghrib with 'Isha) according to the rules of their school; a sick person who cannot stand may pray sitting, and if unable to sit may pray lying down, using gestures; if water would harm them they may perform tayammum; prayer is never dropped completely while a person is conscious.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: shortening 4-unit prayers to 2; Fajr and Maghrib unchanged; combining prayers; sitting if unable to stand; lying down / gestures; tayammum if water harmful; prayer still required.

parts.text: Calculate how many obligatory rak'at a traveller prays in one full day when shortening, and how many fewer this is than the usual 17.
parts.answer: 11 rak'at (2 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 2); 6 fewer than 17.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What do these concessions show about Islam?
parts.answer: That God makes religion easy and does not burden a person beyond their capacity.
parts.working: 1 mark: ease / no undue hardship.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain when a Muslim may perform tayammum and describe how it is done.
parts.answer: It is allowed when water is not available, or not enough for drinking and wudu, or when using water would cause harm through illness or extreme cold; the person makes the intention, strikes clean earth or dust with the palms, and wipes the face and then the hands (Sura 5.6 and 4.43 permit it); it is cancelled when water becomes available or by anything that breaks wudu.

parts.answer: They should perform tayammum with clean earth and pray on time, facing the qibla as best they can (using a compass or the sun) and may shorten if they qualify as travellers; this shows that prayer must not be missed, and that Islam provides practical ways to keep it in any situation.
parts.working: 1 mark: tayammum; 1 mark: pray on time / find qibla; 1 mark: possible shortening; 1 mark: lesson (prayer never abandoned / Islam is practical).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the times of the five daily prayers change through the year and are different in different cities.
parts.answer: The prayer times are set by the position of the sun, not by the clock: Fajr at true dawn, Zuhr after the sun passes its highest point, 'Asr when shadows grow long, Maghrib after sunset and 'Isha when twilight has gone; the length of day and night changes with the seasons, so the times move through the year; cities further west, such as Karachi compared with Lahore, see dawn and sunset later, and cities further north have bigger seasonal changes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: times fixed by the sun's position; correct link for at least two prayers (dawn, zenith, shadows, sunset, end of twilight); seasonal change in day length; east–west position changes the clock time; north–south position changes day length.

parts.answer: Timetables let people plan work, school and travel around prayers when they cannot see the sky clearly; in the far north the sun hardly sets in summer, so twilight may not disappear and scholars have to advise on how to fix 'Isha and Fajr (e.g. by following the nearest normal location or Makka).
parts.working: 1 mark for a benefit of timetables; 1 mark for the far-north difficulty (very short/no night, twilight persists).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how regular prayer can change a Muslim's character and behaviour.
parts.answer: The Qur'an says prayer restrains a person from shameful and wrong deeds (Sura 29.45); remembering God five times a day reminds a person they are accountable; regular timings build discipline and punctuality; purity before prayer encourages cleanliness; standing in rows builds humility and equality; asking forgiveness in prayer encourages honesty about faults; patience and prayer are described as sources of help (Sura 2.45).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four developed points (restrains from wrong; accountability; discipline; cleanliness; humility; seeking help through patience and prayer).

parts.label: b

parts.answer: The fault is not in prayer but in how it is performed: prayer without attention and sincerity has little effect, and the Qur'an condemns those who are heedless of their prayer; when prayed with understanding and humility it does affect behaviour, as the Qur'an promises; so prayer is a powerful means of change but needs sincere effort; a judgement is required.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the change of the qibla from Jerusalem to the Ka'ba.
parts.answer: In Makka and for the first months in Madina the Muslims prayed facing Jerusalem; about sixteen to seventeen months after the migration, verses were revealed telling the Prophet (pbuh) to turn his face towards the Sacred Mosque in Makka (Sura 2.144); the Prophet (pbuh) had hoped for this; some Muslims who heard the news turned during their prayer; opponents criticised the change, and the Qur'an answered that East and West belong to God and that the change was a test of who follows the Messenger.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: first qibla Jerusalem; change about 16–17 months after hijra; Qur'anic command (2.144); Prophet's wish; Muslims turned during prayer; criticism answered (East and West belong to God); a test of obedience.

parts.answer: It unites Muslims everywhere in one direction, from Indonesia to Canada, showing one community worshipping one God; it links them to Ibrahim and Isma'il who built the Ka'ba; it shows obedience to God's command; it gives a sense of belonging and discipline; it does not mean worshipping the Ka'ba, as Muslims worship only God.
parts.working: 1 mark per developed point up to 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the prayers on the two Eids and the prayer at a funeral (janaza).
parts.answer: Eid prayers: offered in congregation in the morning of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, often in an open ground; two units with extra calls of 'God is Greatest'; no call to prayer is made; a sermon is given by the imam; Muslims wear their best clothes. Funeral prayer: a congregational prayer for a dead Muslim, offered standing with the body in front of the imam; there is no bowing or prostration; it includes praising God, blessings on the Prophet (pbuh) and prayers for forgiveness for the dead person; it is a communal duty.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for Eid prayer (time/place, two units with extra takbirs, no adhan, sermon) and up to 2 marks for funeral prayer (standing only, no bowing/prostration, prayers for the dead, communal duty).

parts.answer: He can learn the prayer times for his shift, use short breaks to pray in the hospital prayer room, ask his supervisor for a few minutes at prayer times, and set reminders; prayer brings calm and strength in stressful work and keeps him connected to God; showing commitment can also inspire colleagues.
parts.working: 1 mark per developed practical suggestion (max 2) and 1 mark per reason why it matters (max 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the formal prayer (salat) and personal supplication (du'a).
parts.answer: Salat is obligatory at fixed times, with set conditions (purity, facing the qibla), fixed words and actions in Arabic, and can be in congregation; du'a is a personal request or conversation with God that can be made at any time, in any language and any position, with no set form; du'a is also part of salat (e.g. in sujud and at the end), and the Prophet (pbuh) described du'a as the essence of worship.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: salat obligatory/fixed times; set conditions and form; Arabic recitation/congregation; du'a any time/language/place; du'a no fixed form; du'a included within salat; both are worship.

parts.answer: Some agree because sincerity and understanding matter, and du'a expresses personal needs; but salat is commanded by God and cannot be replaced by du'a; the fixed form unites Muslims everywhere and teaches discipline; the answer is to learn the meaning of what is recited in salat so that it becomes heartfelt too, and to use du'a as well, not instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main rites of hajj from the 8th to the 10th of Dhu al-Hijja.
parts.answer: Pilgrims in ihram go to Mina on the 8th and pray there; on the 9th they go to the plain of 'Arafat and stand in prayer and supplication from midday to sunset (the most important rite); after sunset they go to Muzdalifa, pray and spend the night, and collect pebbles; on the 10th they throw seven pebbles at the large pillar (Jamrat al-'Aqaba) in Mina; they offer an animal sacrifice; men shave or shorten their hair and women cut a lock of hair; they return to Makka for the tawaf al-ifada around the Ka'ba (and the sa'i between Safa and Marwa if not done earlier).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe ihram and the restrictions it places on the pilgrim.
parts.answer: Ihram is the sacred state entered before reaching the miqat (boundary points) for hajj or 'umra, with the intention and the call of response to God (talbiya); men wear two plain, unstitched white sheets and women wear simple modest clothing with the face and hands uncovered; restrictions include: no cutting hair or nails, no perfume, no hunting, no cutting plants in the sacred area, no marriage contracts or marital relations, no quarrelling or bad language; men may not cover their heads.

parts.answer: Everyone looks the same, so differences of wealth, nationality and status disappear; it reminds them of the burial shroud and the Day of Judgement; it encourages humility and focus on God rather than appearance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the pilgrim performs tawaf and sa'y.
parts.answer: Tawaf: the pilgrim, in a state of purity, walks seven times anticlockwise around the Ka'ba with the Ka'ba on the left, starting and ending at the Black Stone, which is kissed, touched or pointed to at each round; men in ihram uncover the right shoulder and walk briskly in the first three rounds of the arrival tawaf; prayers and du'a are made throughout; two rak'at are prayed near the Station of Ibrahim; Zamzam water is drunk. Sa'y: the pilgrim walks seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, starting at Safa and ending at Marwa, with men jogging between the green markers, recalling Hajar's search for water for Isma'il. Tawaf is performed on arrival, as the essential tawaf al-ifada after the 10th, and as a farewell tawaf before leaving Makka.

parts.answer: Ibrahim and his son Isma'il raised the foundations of the House and prayed for it to be accepted (Sura 2.127); Ibrahim called people to pilgrimage; over time the Arabs filled it with idols, about 360 by the Prophet's time, while keeping some rites of hajj; before prophethood the Quraysh rebuilt it and, when the clans quarrelled over who should replace the Black Stone, the young Muhammad (pbuh) placed it on a cloak so all the leaders could lift it together and set it in place himself; Muslims first faced Jerusalem in prayer and then the qibla was changed to the Ka'ba; after Hudaybiya the Muslims performed 'umra; at the conquest of Makka in 630 CE the Prophet (pbuh) cleared and destroyed the idols and Bilal gave the call to prayer from the Ka'ba.

parts.text: Write about the importance of the Day of 'Arafa for pilgrims.
parts.answer: On the 9th of Dhu al-Hijja pilgrims stand on the plain of 'Arafat from after midday until sunset; the Prophet (pbuh) taught that hajj is 'Arafa, so a pilgrim who misses it has missed the hajj; pilgrims spend the time in prayer, supplication and asking forgiveness; it was here that the Prophet (pbuh) gave his Farewell Sermon in 632 CE, and the verse saying the religion had been perfected was revealed; it reminds pilgrims of standing before God on the Day of Judgement (but is not to be confused with it).

parts.answer: e.g. all people are equal, no Arab is better than a non-Arab, nor white than black, except by piety, which challenges racism today; the rights of women must be respected and husbands must treat wives kindly, relevant to family life; lives, property and honour are sacred, relevant to crime and corruption; interest was abolished, relevant to finance.

parts.answer: It is performed on the 10th of Dhu al-Hijja after the Eid prayer, and on the following days of Eid, by pilgrims and by Muslims around the world who can afford it; a healthy animal of the right age (sheep, goat, cow or camel) is slaughtered in God's name, humanely; a common recommended practice is to keep a third of the meat, give a third to relatives and friends and a third to the poor; it recalls Ibrahim's obedience; the Qur'an says it is not the meat or the blood that reaches God but the believers' piety (Sura 22.37).

parts.answer: Leaves on the 12th: 7 + 21 + 21 = 49 pebbles. Stays for the 13th: 49 + 21 = 70 pebbles.

parts.label: c

parts.answer: It is a symbolic, repeated rejection of evil, reminding Muslims that temptation must be resisted again and again, e.g. refusing to cheat or to waste time on harmful content, and that God's help is sought in doing so.

parts.text: Explain the lessons that hajj teaches about equality and unity of the Muslim community.
parts.answer: Millions of Muslims of every race, nation and language gather in one place at one time; all wear the same simple clothing, so rich and poor cannot be told apart; all perform the same rites in the same order, facing the same Ka'ba; they pray together and share hardships; the Farewell Sermon stresses that no one is superior except by piety; pilgrims return with a sense of a worldwide brotherhood.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the differences between hajj and 'umra.
parts.answer: Hajj is a pillar of Islam, obligatory once in a lifetime for those able; 'umra is not a pillar: most Hanafi and Maliki scholars regard it as a strongly recommended Sunna, while Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars hold it obligatory once in a lifetime; hajj can only be performed on fixed days in Dhu al-Hijja, while 'umra may be done at any time of year; hajj includes standing at 'Arafat, the nights at Muzdalifa and Mina, the stoning and the sacrifice; 'umra consists of ihram, tawaf, sa'i and shaving or cutting the hair, and takes only a few hours.

parts.answer: Tamattu': the pilgrim performs 'umra in the hajj months, leaves ihram, then enters ihram again for hajj on the 8th of Dhu al-Hijja, and must offer a sacrifice; qiran: 'umra and hajj are combined in one ihram without leaving it in between, and a sacrifice is required; ifrad: hajj alone, in one ihram, with no 'umra and no required sacrifice (though one may be offered voluntarily).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how Muslims celebrate Eid al-Fitr.
parts.answer: It is celebrated on the 1st of Shawwal, at the end of Ramadan, when the new moon is sighted; before the Eid prayer each household pays zakat al-fitr (a set amount of staple food or its value for each member) to the poor; Muslims bathe, wear new or best clothes and often eat something sweet before going to the prayer; they say 'God is Greatest' on the way; they attend the Eid prayer and sermon in congregation; they greet each other, visit relatives and friends, give gifts to children (eidi) and share food.

parts.answer: It purifies the fasting person from any idle or bad talk during Ramadan; it ensures the poor can also celebrate Eid and have food on the day; it reminds the community that celebration must include everyone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the celebration of Eid al-Adha.
parts.answer: It takes place on the 10th of Dhu al-Hijja, during the hajj; Muslims attend the Eid prayer in congregation in the morning; those who can afford it sacrifice an animal after the prayer, in memory of Ibrahim's obedience; the meat is shared with family, friends and the poor; people repeat 'God is Greatest' during the days of Eid; families visit one another and celebrate for several days.

parts.text: Write about the Day of 'Ashura and the reasons it is significant for Muslims.
parts.answer: It is the 10th of Muharram; when the Prophet (pbuh) arrived in Madina he learned that the Jews fasted on this day to remember God saving the Prophet Musa and his people from Pharaoh; he fasted on it and encouraged Muslims to fast; later Ramadan became the obligatory fast and the 'Ashura fast remained voluntary; it is also the day on which Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet (pbuh), was martyred at Karbala in 680 CE, which Muslims, and especially Shi'a Muslims, remember with mourning and gatherings.

parts.answer: It is due from every Muslim who has more than their basic needs on the day of Eid al-Fitr; the head of the household pays on behalf of each dependant, including children; the amount is about one sa' (a set measure) of staple food or its value; it should be paid before the Eid prayer, and may be paid a day or two earlier so that it reaches the poor in time; if paid after the prayer it counts only as ordinary charity.

parts.text: Explain how the start of Ramadan and the dates of the two Eids are decided.
parts.answer: The Islamic months are lunar and begin when the new crescent moon is sighted after sunset on the 29th; if it is not seen, the month is completed as 30 days; the Prophet (pbuh) told Muslims to fast on seeing the moon and end the fast on seeing it; in Pakistan an official moon-sighting committee (the Ruet-e-Hilal Committee) gathers reports and announces the decision; because sighting depends on place and weather, different countries may begin on different days.

parts.answer: It was introduced during the caliphate of 'Umar, who, after consulting the Companions, chose the year of the migration (622 CE) as its starting point; it is a lunar calendar of twelve months, each beginning with the sighting of the new moon; the year begins with Muharram; months include Ramadan (fasting), Shawwal (Eid al-Fitr) and Dhu al-Hijja (hajj and Eid al-Adha); a lunar year is about 354 days.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why do you think it helps a reader today to know whether a passage was revealed in Makka or in Madina?
parts.answer: It explains the situation the verses addressed (a persecuted minority or an organised community), so the reader understands their meaning and applies them correctly, for example patience in hardship from Makkan verses and social rules from Madinan verses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Qur'an was revealed gradually over about 23 years. Give reasons for this gradual revelation.
parts.answer: To strengthen the heart of the Prophet (pbuh) through continuing contact with God during persecution (the Qur'an itself answers the objection of why it was not sent all at once, Sura 25.32); so that it could be memorised and written down easily; so that verses could answer events and questions as they happened; so that laws could be introduced step by step, for example alcohol was forbidden in stages; to allow the new Muslims to change their habits gradually; to challenge the opponents repeatedly with new verses.
parts.working: Indicative content: Strengthen/comfort the Prophet (pbuh); easier to memorise/record; responded to events/questions; gradual introduction of laws; alcohol in stages as example; people could change gradually; continuing challenge to opponents; time for understanding and practice. parts.label: b
parts.text: How can the gradual way the Qur'an was revealed guide a teacher or parent today?
parts.answer: Change is best brought step by step; a teacher or parent should introduce good habits (e.g. regular prayer for a child) gradually with patience and explanation, rather than demanding everything at once, so that the habit lasts.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Principle (gradual, patient change); practical application; reason/judgement (lasting change, less resistance). parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the experiences of the Prophet (pbuh) when revelation came upon him, as reported by those who were with him.
parts.answer: He sometimes heard a sound like a ringing bell; he became very heavy (a camel he rode would kneel under the weight); his forehead sweated even on cold days; his face changed colour; he seemed absorbed and unaware of his surroundings; afterwards he recited the words he had received clearly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: sound like a bell; heaviness (camel knelt / pressure on a Companion's thigh); sweating on cold days; change of face/colour; absorbed, cut off from surroundings; afterwards recited exactly what he received.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A friend in Karachi says the Qur'an is just a wise book written by a good man. Using the experience of revelation, how might a Muslim respond politely?
parts.answer: A Muslim could explain calmly that the Prophet (pbuh) did not control when or how revelation came, that its arrival was a heavy physical experience, and that he himself distinguished it from his own words (his Hadith), so Muslims believe it is the word of God; the reply should be respectful and invite further discussion.
parts.working: 1 mark: Prophet (pbuh) did not control revelation; 1 mark: distinction between Qur'an and his own sayings / physical signs; 1 mark: respectful manner of response (wisdom and good speech).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Surah al-Muddaththir (74) opens with a command to the Prophet (pbuh). State the command in your own words.
parts.answer: He was told to get up and warn people.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'get up' or 'rise'; 1 mark for 'warn' (deliver a warning).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the warning was about in the early Makkan period, and why delivering it needed courage.
parts.answer: The warning called people to worship God alone, to give up false gods, and to remember the Day of Judgement and accountability. It was dangerous because the Makkan leaders opposed the Prophet (pbuh) and his followers, mocked and pressured them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: warning against polytheism or disbelief; calling people to worship God alone; reminding them of the Day of Judgement; a clear example of opposition (mockery, insults, pressure on believers). Maximum 4 marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Qur'an refers to the earlier scriptures. Name the scripture revealed to Prophet Musa (Moses), the one revealed to Prophet Dawud (David) and the one revealed to Prophet 'Isa (Jesus).
parts.answer: Taurat (Torah) to Musa; Zabur (Psalms) to Dawud; Injil (Gospel) to 'Isa.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the correct scripture and prophet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the Qur'an says about its relationship to these earlier revelations.

Maximum 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by wahy (revelation) in Islam.
parts.answer: Wahy is God's communication of His message to a chosen prophet. The prophet receives it from God, not through his own effort, and passes it on to people. The Qur'an is the revealed word of God that came through the angel Jibril and other means.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: communication from God; given to chosen prophets; received not through human effort; passed on to people; the Qur'an is the word of God revealed through Jibril. Maximum 4.

parts.text: State one feature of the Qur'an that the Prophet's (pbuh) sayings in the Hadith do not share.
parts.answer: The Qur'an is recited as part of the daily prayers, while the Hadiths are not recited in worship in the same way.
parts.working: 1 mark for recitation in prayer; 1 mark for a sound contrast (the Qur'an's words are preserved exactly as revealed; the Hadiths are reported, often in the narrator's own words).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Surah al-Qiyamah (75:16–19) describes an instruction given to the Prophet (pbuh) while revelation was coming to him. Describe the instruction.
parts.answer: He was told not to hurry to move his tongue to memorise the revelation. God would gather it for him, enable him to recite it, and then make its meaning clear.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: not to hurry or move his tongue quickly; God will gather the revelation; God will make him able to recite it; God will explain it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this teaches Muslims who are learning to memorise the Qur'an today.
parts.answer: Learners should be patient and steady, trusting that God helps them. They should learn with a teacher, revise regularly and not rush through the recitation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: patience and steady practice; trust in God's help; learning under a teacher; regular revision; avoid rushing and reciting carelessly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pause in revelation (fatra) after the first revelation, and the revelation that ended it.
parts.answer: After the first revelation there was a period when no more verses came; the Prophet (pbuh) was deeply worried and distressed, unsure whether he would receive revelation again; then he saw the angel again between the sky and the earth and was frightened, went home and asked to be wrapped; the opening verses of Sura 74 (al-Muddaththir) were revealed, telling the one wrapped in a cloak to arise and warn, glorify his Lord, keep clean and avoid idols; after this revelation came regularly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: revelation stopped for a time; Prophet (pbuh) anxious/sad; saw the angel again (between sky and earth); returned home and asked to be covered; Sura 74 revealed; command to arise and warn; glorify the Lord / purify clothes / avoid idols; revelation continued regularly afterwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The pause in revelation shows that the Prophet (pbuh) could not produce the Qur'an himself.' To what extent do you agree? Give reasons.
parts.answer: Agree largely: if he were the author he could have continued at will, yet he waited anxiously and was distressed; the timing of revelation was outside his control, which supports Muslim belief that it came from God. A balanced answer may add that the pause also prepared him for the mission and that belief rests on many other signs too (its content, his honesty), so it is one strong piece of evidence among others.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Prophet's opponents in Makka reacted to the revelations, and how the Qur'an responded to their claims.
parts.answer: They rejected the message and mocked it; they called the Prophet (pbuh) a poet, a soothsayer (kahin), a madman or a sorcerer; they said the verses were only 'tales of the ancients' or that a foreign man was teaching him; they demanded miracles instead; the Qur'an denied each claim (e.g. it is not the word of a poet or a soothsayer, Sura 69.41–42; the man they point to speaks a foreign tongue while the Qur'an is in clear Arabic, Sura 16.103); it challenged them to produce a book like it, then ten suras, then even one sura like it (e.g. Sura 2.23, 11.13), and they could not.

parts.text: Why do Muslims see the failure of the Arabs to meet the Qur'an's challenge as evidence that it comes from God?
parts.answer: The Makkans were masters of Arabic poetry and eloquence and were desperate to defeat the message, yet none could produce even one sura like it; the Prophet (pbuh) was not known as a poet and could not read or write; so Muslims see its unmatched language and content (its inimitability) as a sign that it is God's word, not human composition.

parts.answer: Because it is hidden, Muslims make extra effort across several nights rather than one, which increases worship, sincerity and self-discipline; it keeps believers hopeful and humble; communities in mosques from Lahore to London fill the last ten nights with prayer, so the whole end of Ramadan becomes a time of spiritual effort.

parts.text: Surah al-Anfal (8:1) opens with a question about the spoils (anfal) of a battle. Name the surah and verse, and name the battle the verse is linked to.
parts.answer: Surah al-Anfal (8), verse 1; the battle of Badr.
parts.working: 1 mark for surah and verse; 1 mark for the battle of Badr.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the verse teaches about how the spoils should be handled and why the answer came from God.
parts.answer: The spoils belong to God and His Messenger, who decide how they are divided. Believers should be conscious of God, settle their disputes by putting things right among themselves, and obey God and His Messenger. The answer was given because the Companions disagreed about the division.

parts.working: 1 mark for revelation responding to a question; 1 mark for responding to a dispute; 1 mark for guidance that was practical for the community; 1 mark for a clear link to the Qur'an's role as guidance for every situation. Maximum 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the claim that the Qur'an is inimitable (i'jaz) and why Muslims see this as a sign of its divine origin.
parts.answer: A structured account of the challenge in the Qur'an to produce something like it (for example 2:23 and 10:38), the failure of the Arab poets and orators of the time to do so, the qualities of its style, its legislation, its prophecies and its lasting effect, and why Muslims take these as signs of divine origin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what naskh (abrogation) means in the study of the Qur'an.
parts.answer: Naskh is the view that a later ruling or verse replaces an earlier one, so the earlier ruling is no longer applied. Qur'an 2:106 refers to God replacing a verse with one better or similar.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: a later ruling replaces an earlier one; the principle is linked to 2:106; the replaced ruling is no longer applied in law; it is a question of which ruling is in force.

parts.text: Describe how the Qur'an was preserved during the lifetime of the Prophet (pbuh).
parts.answer: Revelations were memorised by the Prophet (pbuh) and by many Companions (huffaz) and recited in daily prayers; they were written down by scribes such as Zayd ibn Thabit, 'Ali and Ubayy ibn Ka'b on materials such as palm leaves, flat stones, animal bones, leather and parchment; the Prophet (pbuh) told the scribes the position of each verse; he checked what was written; Jibril reviewed the revelation with him each Ramadan, twice in the last year; but it was not yet gathered into one volume because revelation was still continuing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps the caliph 'Uthman took to produce standard copies of the Qur'an.
parts.answer: Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, returning from campaigns in Armenia and Azerbaijan, reported that Muslims from different regions were disputing about how the Qur'an was recited; 'Uthman consulted senior Companions; he borrowed Abu Bakr's sheets from Hafsa; he formed a committee led by Zayd ibn Thabit with 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn al-'As and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith; he told them to write in the dialect of the Quraysh where they differed, as it was revealed in that dialect; copies were made and sent to the main centres of the Muslim lands, with one kept in Madina; other private copies were ordered to be burned; Hafsa's sheets were returned to her.
parts.working: Indicative content: Hudhayfa's report; disputes over recitation in newly conquered lands; consultation; Hafsa's copy borrowed; committee/Zayd as head; one other committee member named; Quraysh dialect rule; copies sent to provinces (one kept in Madina); other copies destroyed; Hafsa's copy returned; title 'Jami' al-Qur'an' (gatherer of the Qur'an). parts.answer: Yes, most Muslims agree he was right: the Companions agreed with him, and it removed the cause of division so that all Muslims read the same text, which has kept the community united to this day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the order of the suras and verses in the Qur'an and explain who decided it.
parts.answer: The Qur'an is not arranged in the order of revelation; it begins with Sura al-Fatiha and then, broadly, the long suras come first and the short ones at the end; the position of each verse within its sura was set by the Prophet (pbuh), who told the scribes where to place new verses, as guided by Jibril; this order was confirmed in the yearly reviews and was kept in the written collections.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The first revelation (Sura 96) is near the end of the Qur'an, not at the start. Why does this not cause problems for Muslims reading the Qur'an?
parts.answer: Muslims believe the order itself is from God through the Prophet (pbuh), and each sura carries complete guidance; knowledge of when verses were revealed is available from scholars, so the reader can still learn their background.

parts.answer: The Qur'an states that God Himself revealed the Reminder and will guard it (Sura 15.9); it says it is easy to remember (repeated in Sura 54); the Prophet (pbuh) encouraged learning and teaching the Qur'an, saying the best of people are those who learn it and teach it; he praised those who recite it skilfully and promised reward for each letter recited.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: God promises to protect it (15.9); made easy to remember (Sura 54); best are those who learn and teach it; reward for reciting; skilful reciters praised; encouragement to recite in prayer / at night.

parts.answer: It keeps the text preserved in many people, continuing the method of the Companions; it provides imams and leaders for tarawih and daily prayers; it builds discipline and a strong link with the Qur'an in young people, and when combined with study of meaning it shapes good character in society.

parts.answer: 0.83 juz per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Qur'an forbade alcohol in stages. Describe these stages.
parts.answer: First, it said wine and gambling contain some benefit but their sin is greater (Sura 2.219); next, believers were told not to come to prayer while intoxicated (Sura 4.43); finally, intoxicants and gambling were declared a filthy work of Satan to be avoided completely (Sura 5.90–91); the Companions poured away their wine so that it ran in the streets of Madina.
parts.working: 1 mark per stage (3 stages) and 1 mark for the Companions' response or for correct references. Maximum 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What principle of law-making does this show, and how could it guide a government in a Muslim country today?
parts.answer: It shows gradualness and wisdom: people were prepared step by step, with reasons given, before a full ban; a government could introduce reforms (e.g. reducing smoking or drug use, ending interest in banking) in stages with education and support so that people accept and keep them.
parts.working: 1 mark: principle (gradual / with reasons); 1 mark: explanation of why it works; 1–2 marks: modern application with example.

practice.subtopic: The Qur'an as a source of Islamic law

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Muslim jurists use the Qur'an when a modern practice is not mentioned in it by name, such as a new online betting game.
parts.answer: They search the Qur'an and Sunna for related rulings: the Qur'an forbids gambling (maysir) together with intoxicants as the work of Satan (Sura 5.90–91); they identify what makes maysir forbidden (gaining money by pure chance at another's loss, which causes enmity and distracts from God); they check whether the new game has the same features — if it does, the same ruling applies whatever its form (qiyas); they also consider general Qur'anic principles such as not consuming others' wealth unjustly (Sura 4.29) and avoiding harm and waste; they look for agreement among scholars (ijma').
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: look first for direct text (5.90–91 on gambling); identify the cause/features of the original ruling; apply the ruling to the new case with the same features (analogy); general principles (no unjust taking of wealth, avoid harm/waste); consensus of scholars.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why is it important that such rulings are made by qualified scholars rather than by individuals for themselves?
parts.answer: Scholars know Arabic, the Qur'an and Sunna, earlier rulings and the methods of reasoning; this prevents mistakes and rulings based on personal desire; agreed rulings keep the community united; individuals may still study and ask questions, but final rulings need expertise, as in medicine or engineering.
parts.working: 1 mark per developed reason, up to 4: expertise/knowledge; avoid error/desire; unity of community; analogy with other expert fields.

parts.answer: Surah al-Baqarah (2), verse 282.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two rules from this verse about recording a debt.
parts.answer: The debt should be written down, with a fair scribe who writes what is agreed. The debtor dictates the terms. Two witnesses should be present, either two men or one man and two women. The scribe must not refuse to write.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: write the debt down; a fair scribe writes it; the debtor dictates; two witnesses (two men, or a man and two women); the scribe must not refuse; the terms must be clear. Maximum 4 marks.

parts.label: c

parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: a written record prevents disputes; the creditor's right is protected; the debtor is protected from false claims; both sides can check the terms; witnesses give fairness and trust.

practice.stem: A man dies. His estate, after debts and funeral costs are paid, is Rs 3,000. There is no spouse, no parents and no will. His only heirs are one son and one daughter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the share of the son.
parts.answer: Rs 2,000. The son receives two parts and the daughter one part, so each part is Rs 1,000.

parts.working: 1 part of 3 = 1,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the meaning of qiyas (analogy) and how it is based on the Qur'an. Give an example.
parts.answer: Qiyas is applying a ruling from the Qur'an or Sunna to a new case that has the same underlying reason (cause, 'illa); it is used only when the Qur'an and Sunna have no direct ruling and there is no consensus; example: the Qur'an forbids wine (khamr) because it intoxicates and leads people away from remembering God (Sura 5.90–91), so scholars apply the same ruling to other intoxicants such as harmful drugs; another example: the Qur'an tells believers to leave trade at the call to Friday prayer (Sura 62.9), so other activities that distract from it are also not allowed at that time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give examples of concessions (rulings that make things easier in hardship) found in the Qur'an.
parts.answer: A sick person or traveller may miss fasts in Ramadan and make them up later, and those who cannot fast may feed a poor person instead (Sura 2.184–185); travellers may shorten prayers when on a journey (Sura 4.101); when water is not available or would cause harm, tayammum with clean earth replaces washing (Sura 4.43, 5.6); a person forced by necessity may eat otherwise forbidden food to stay alive (Sura 2.173); hajj is required only of those who are able (Sura 3.97); a person forced to deny faith under threat is excused while the heart remains firm (Sura 16.106).

parts.text: Write about the Names and Attributes of God, giving the meanings of at least four of His names.
parts.answer: God has many beautiful names (al-asma' al-husna), traditionally ninety-nine, which describe His perfect qualities. His attributes are perfect and unlike those of creation.

parts.answer: It invites people to reflect on the creation of the heavens and earth, the alternation of night and day, the sun and moon, rain bringing dead land to life, plants and fruits, animals and the creation of humans; the order and balance in creation show a single Creator; if there were more than one god there would be disorder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Prophet's (pbuh) mission in Makka was a struggle to restore belief in one God against idol worship.
parts.answer: The Makkans had filled the Ka'ba of Ibrahim with idols; the early suras called people to worship God alone, rejected idols as powerless, and reminded them that Allah, whom they acknowledged as Creator, alone deserved worship; the Quraysh opposed this as it threatened their religion, status and trade; Sura 109 rejected any compromise in worship and Sura 112 defined God's nature; the struggle ended with the idols being destroyed at the conquest of Makka.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): the Ka'ba was built by Ibrahim and Isma'il for the worship of one God; idols such as Hubal, al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat had been introduced; the Makkans believed in Allah as creator but worshipped idols as intermediaries; the Prophet's (pbuh) first public message was 'there is no god but God'; the Qur'an showed idols could not create, hear or help; the Quraysh feared loss of pilgrim trade and leadership; offers of compromise were rejected (Sura 109); Sura 112 answered questions about God's nature; believers like Bilal suffered for saying 'One'; the struggle continued in Madina; at the conquest of Makka the 360 idols were destroyed and the Ka'ba restored to tawhid. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.answer: Disagree: shirk can take new forms such as worshipping wealth, fame, power or one's own desires (45.23), and superstition; tawhid remains the foundation of worship and morality.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how belief in tawhid should shape a Muslim's attitude towards the natural environment, referring to the ideas of khilafa (stewardship) and amana (trust).
parts.answer: Because the One God created everything and owns it, nature is His creation and a sign of Him; humans are His trustees (khalifa, 2.30) holding the earth as a trust, so they must use it responsibly, not waste (7.31) or spread corruption, and will be accountable.

Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how belief in tawhid affects Muslim society as a whole.
parts.answer: If there is one Creator, all humans are equal before Him, so racism and class pride are rejected; it unites Muslims as one ummah with one direction of prayer; laws come from the one God, so justice applies equally to rich and poor; leaders are accountable to God; it encourages brotherhood and care for the weak.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Islam forbids practices such as fortune-telling, belief in bad omens and reading horoscopes, in the light of tawhid.
parts.answer: Only God knows the unseen (6.59, 27.65) and controls fate; such practices claim knowledge or power that belongs to God alone, make people rely on other than God, spread fear and can lead to shirk; the Prophet (pbuh) rejected bad omens and warned against going to fortune-tellers.

Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.text: Describe the mission of the Prophet Nuh (Noah) as told in the Qur'an.
parts.answer: Nuh preached to his people for a very long time (950 years, 29.14), calling them to worship God; most rejected and mocked him; he built the ark by God's command; the believers and animals were saved and the disbelievers, including his son, were drowned.

parts.answer: To keep advising patiently for a long time, using different methods, without giving up, and leave results to God.

parts.answer: A nabi is a prophet who receives revelation from God; a rasul is a messenger who is also given a message or law to deliver, often with a book; every messenger is a prophet but not every prophet is a messenger. The ulu'l-'azm are the great messengers known for their patience and determination: Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus and Muhammad (pbuh).

Ulu'l-'azm means 'possessors of firm resolve / great patience'; they are Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, 'Isa and Muhammad (pbuh), with an example of the patience of each. practice.subtopic: Life after death and the Day of Judgement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what Muslims believe about the end of the world (the Hour, al-Sa'a).
parts.answer: Only God knows when the Hour will come; there will be signs before it; the trumpet will be blown by the angel Israfil; the universe will be destroyed — mountains crumble, seas boil, stars fall (Suras 81, 82, 99, 101); all living things will die; at a second blast all will be resurrected for judgement.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): knowledge of the Hour is with God alone (31.34; 7.187); it will come suddenly; minor and major signs taught in Hadith (e.g. spread of ignorance and dishonesty, building tall buildings by former herders; major signs such as the sun rising from the west); the first blowing of the trumpet; the earth shaken and bringing out its burdens (Sura 99); mountains like scattered wool and people like scattered moths (Sura 101); sky split, stars scattered, seas made to overflow (Suras 81, 82); everything perishes except God (55.26–27); second blast: resurrection of all. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why do you think God has kept the time of the Hour secret? Explain.
parts.answer: So that people always stay ready, repent without delay and do good continuously, rather than waiting until the last moment.
parts.working: Points may include: constant readiness; test of faith in the unseen; avoid panic or complacency; one's own death is also unknown; encourages repentance now. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Life after death and the Day of Judgement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what Muslims believe about the book of deeds, the scales (mizan) and the bridge (sirat) on the Day of Judgement.
parts.answer: Each person receives the record of their deeds; the righteous in the right hand, the wicked in the left or behind the back; deeds are weighed on the scales and even an atom's weight counts; all must cross the bridge over Hell, the righteous crossing safely.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: record kept by the recording angels; given in right hand (successful) or left hand (losers) (69.19–29); people will be asked to read their own book (17.14); the scales weigh deeds with complete justice (21.47); heavy scales lead to Paradise (101.6–9); atom's weight of good or evil seen (99.7–8); the sirat over Hell, crossed at speeds according to deeds; some fall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how belief in the scales could encourage a Muslim student to keep doing small good deeds.
parts.answer: Since even the smallest deed is weighed and counts, small acts like smiling, helping a classmate or removing litter are worthwhile and may tip the balance.
parts.working: Points may include: atom's weight (99.7); good deeds wipe out bad (11.114); consistency loved by God; intention multiplies reward; examples from school life. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Life after death and the Day of Judgement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the Day of Judgement shows both God's justice and His mercy.
parts.answer: Justice: every deed is recorded and weighed exactly, no one bears another's burden, no one is wronged even slightly, witnesses including limbs testify. Mercy: good deeds are multiplied and bad deeds counted once, repentance wipes sins, intercession by God's permission, God's mercy exceeds His anger.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): justice: complete record; scales (21.47); no soul bears another's burden (6.164); body parts witness (36.65; 24.24); wrongdoers repay victims; nothing hidden. Mercy: a good deed rewarded at least tenfold and evil only once (6.160); intention to do good counts; repentance accepted until death; God forgives all sins for those who turn to Him (39.53); intercession with His permission (2.255); God's mercy encompasses everything (7.156); Hadith that God's mercy prevails over His anger. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how belief in the Day of Judgement should affect the way a Muslim employer treats the workers under them.
parts.answer: The employer will be held accountable for every wage and right, so they should pay fairly and on time, avoid exploitation and treat workers with respect, because God will judge every wrong done to them.
parts.working: Points may include: accountability for every act (21.47; 99.7–8); the Prophet's teaching to pay a worker before his sweat dries; fair wages and written contracts; exploiting the weak will be judged; justice and mercy together; a practical example such as brick-kiln or domestic workers in Pakistan. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Life after death and the Day of Judgement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what Islam teaches about repentance (tawba) and the time when it is accepted.
parts.answer: Sincere repentance involves regret, stopping the sin, resolving not to return and righting wrongs done to others; God accepts it at any time before the soul reaches the throat at death or before the sun rises from the west.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: God loves those who repent (2.222); never despair of His mercy (39.53); conditions: regret, stopping, intention not to repeat; returning others' rights or seeking their forgiveness; accepted until death throes (4.17–18); repentance replaces bad deeds with good (25.70); the Prophet (pbuh) asked forgiveness many times a day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A young man in Peshawar believes he has sinned too much for God to forgive him. Using belief in the Hereafter, explain how a Muslim friend could help him.
parts.answer: Remind him that God's mercy is greater than any sin, that repentance is open until death, and help him take practical steps to change and make amends.
parts.working: Points may include: 39.53 do not despair; examples of great sinners forgiven; repentance changes record; practical support (prayer, good company); avoid judgemental attitude. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Life after death and the Day of Judgement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why belief in life after death is important for Muslims.
parts.answer: It gives meaning and purpose to life as a test; it guarantees final justice, since many wrongs are not punished in this world; it motivates good deeds and discourages sin; it gives comfort in suffering and loss, as the believer hopes to meet loved ones; it reminds people that wealth and status are temporary; without it, belief in God's justice would be incomplete.
parts.working: Indicative content: Life as a test with a purpose; final justice for wrongs not punished in this world; moral motivation to do good and avoid evil; comfort in suffering and bereavement; worldly things are temporary; accountability for every deed. Level 4 needs several reasons, each developed. Marked by levels out of 10. parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Belief in the Hereafter is the main reason Muslims behave morally.' To what extent do you agree?
parts.answer: Partly: accountability is a strong motive, but Muslims are also moved by love of God, gratitude and concern for others, and many good deeds are done for God's pleasure rather than fear or reward alone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what Muslims believe about barzakh and the questioning in the grave.
parts.answer: Barzakh is the barrier or stage between death and the resurrection; after burial two angels, known in tradition as Munkar and Nakir, question the dead person about who their Lord is, what their religion is and who their prophet was; believers answer correctly and their grave becomes spacious and peaceful; those who rejected faith cannot answer and suffer; the soul remains in this state until the Day of Resurrection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How might belief in the questioning in the grave affect the way a Muslim lives?
parts.answer: It reminds them that faith must be real and lived, not just words, because only sincere belief and practice will allow them to answer; this encourages regular worship and good deeds.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Faith must be genuine; motivates daily worship and good character; urgency — death can come at any time, with example. practice.subtopic: Life after death and the Day of Judgement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the arguments the Qur'an gives for the resurrection of the dead.
parts.answer: The One who created humans the first time can easily recreate them (36.78–79); the earth is dead and God revives it with rain, so He will revive the dead; the creation of the heavens and earth is greater than recreating humans; human development in the womb shows God's power; justice requires a Day when wrongs are put right.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): objectors asked who will revive rotten bones; answer: He who created them the first time (36.78–79); the first creation was from nothing, the second is easier (30.27); revival of dead land by rain (e.g. 22.5; 41.39); stages of human creation from a drop to a full person (22.5; 23.12–14); heavens and earth are a greater creation (40.57); sleep as a lesser death and waking (39.42); justice: good and evil people are not treated the same in this life (38.28); God is All-Powerful. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which of these arguments do you think would be most convincing to a person who doubts life after death today? Give reasons.
parts.answer: Any reasoned choice, e.g. the argument from justice, since many wrongs in this world go unpunished, or from first creation, since science shows the universe had a beginning.
parts.working: Points may include: argued choice; linked to modern thinking; comparison with another argument; recognises faith in the unseen is still required. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Life after death and the Day of Judgement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how belief in the Hereafter should affect a Muslim's attitude towards wealth and the pleasures of this world.
parts.answer: This life is temporary and a test (67.2); wealth is a trust from God to be earned lawfully and spent rightly; it will be questioned; it cannot be taken to the grave; it should be used for good, zakat and charity; pleasures are allowed within limits but must not distract from God (63.9, 102.1–2); the Hereafter is better and lasting (87.17).
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): life as a test and temporary enjoyment (57.20); the Hereafter better and more lasting (87.16–17); wealth and children as a test (8.28); rivalry in increasing wealth distracts until the grave (102.1–2); questioned about how wealth was earned and spent; zakat and sadaqa as investment for the Hereafter; lawful earning; avoid waste and extravagance; enjoy lawful good things (7.32); balance between this world and the next (28.77); the Prophet's (pbuh) simple life. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Belief in the Hereafter makes Muslims neglect their responsibilities in this world.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: Disagree: Islam teaches that the Hereafter is earned through work, family care, justice and service in this world (28.77); neglect would itself be a sin; but some misuse the idea as an excuse.
parts.working: Points may include: 28.77 do not forget your share of this world; work as worship; caring for family and society rewarded; neglect is sinful; possible misunderstanding by some; justified conclusion. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

practice.subtopic: Life after death and the Day of Judgement

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Qur'an describes Paradise and Hell using images from this world, such as gardens, rivers, shade, fire and boiling water. Explain why it uses such images.
parts.answer: Humans can only understand the unseen through what they know; the images make reward and punishment real and vivid to motivate people, while the reality is far greater (32.17: no soul knows what joy is hidden for them).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: humans cannot imagine what they have not experienced; images taken from things valued by the first listeners (shade, water, gardens in the desert); they motivate and warn; they are real, not only symbols, but beyond our full understanding; 32.17 no soul knows what is hidden; the greatest reward is God's pleasure and seeing Him; emotional and moral impact.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The greatest reward of Paradise is not physical pleasure but nearness to God.' Discuss.
parts.answer: Many scholars agree that God's pleasure (9.72 'greater still is God's good pleasure') is the highest reward, though physical rewards are real and also promised.
parts.working: Points may include: 9.72; seeing God; peace and greeting of 'salam'; physical rewards also promised; motive of love rather than only reward; balanced conclusion. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what Muslims believe about the nature of angels.
parts.answer: Angels are created by God from light; they are unseen beings, without free will, who always obey God; they do not eat, drink, marry or tire; they worship and praise God constantly; they can take different forms, including human form, by God's permission; they have different duties; belief in them is an Article of Faith.
parts.working: Indicative content: Created from light; unseen; no free will — always obey; do not sin; no physical needs (food, sleep, family); constant worship; can appear in human form (e.g. Jibril); vast numbers; different duties; belief in angels is part of iman. parts.answer: Knowing angels record every deed and are always present encourages a Muslim to act well even in private, and their obedience is an example of devotion.

parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept 'Malak al-Mawt' for (iii).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Qur'an presents angels as obedient servants of God.
parts.answer: Angels are created from light, have no free will to disobey, do exactly what they are commanded (66.6), never tire of worship and glorify God night and day (21.20), are not daughters of God (refuting the Makkan belief) and are honoured servants (21.26–27) with different duties.

Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why humans, who can disobey God, are given a higher possible status than angels if they choose to obey.
parts.answer: Because their obedience is a free choice made against desires and temptations, which is more of an achievement than the obedience of angels who have no choice.
parts.working: Points may include: free will; struggle against desire and Satan; angels prostrated to Adam; human knowledge (names); responsibility of khilafa; humans can also fall lower by misusing choice. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe ways in which angels are connected with Muslim worship, for example in prayer, Ramadan and gatherings of remembrance.
parts.answer: Angels descend on the Night of Power (97.4); angels attend gatherings where God is remembered; angels pray for forgiveness for those who wait for prayer and record people arriving for Friday prayer; recording angels note every act of worship.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: angels and the Spirit descend on Laylat al-Qadr (97.4–5); angels surround gatherings of dhikr and Qur'an study; angels of night and day meet at fajr and 'asr prayers; angels at the mosque door record those who arrive early for Friday prayer; angels say 'amin' with the worshippers after al-Fatiha; angels pray for those who remain in their prayer place; recording of all deeds.

parts.answer: It encourages sincerity, concentration, punctuality (e.g. arriving early on Friday) and respect for the mosque and gatherings.
parts.working: Points may include: concentration in prayer; arriving early; sincerity; respectful behaviour in the mosque; more effort on the Night of Power. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the part played by angels in the story of the creation of Adam, as told in the Qur'an.
parts.answer: God told the angels He would place a khalifa on earth; they asked whether He would place one who would cause corruption and bloodshed; God said He knew what they did not; He taught Adam the names, and the angels admitted they knew only what He taught them; He commanded them to prostrate to Adam and they all did except Iblis, who was of the jinn and refused out of pride.

parts.text: What does the angels' reply 'we have no knowledge except what You have taught us' teach Muslims about knowledge? Explain.
parts.answer: All knowledge comes from God, so learners should be humble, admit what they do not know and be grateful, not proud like Iblis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the Qur'an says about the help of angels to the Muslims at the Battle of Badr.
parts.answer: When the Muslims prayed for help, God promised to send a thousand angels following one another (8.9); the angels strengthened the believers' hearts, and the help was good news and reassurance, while victory came only from God (8.10); Sura 3 also mentions angels sent to support them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: the Muslims, outnumbered, called on God; the Prophet (pbuh) prayed intensely; God answered with a thousand angels in succession (8.9); it was given as good news and to reassure their hearts (8.10); victory comes only from God; angels told to strengthen the believers (8.12); 3.123–125 also mention angels at Badr; sleep and rain sent to calm them (8.11).

parts.text: Explain why the Qur'an stresses that victory comes only from God even when angels helped.
parts.answer: To keep believers' trust in God alone, not in angels, numbers or weapons; angels act only by His command.
parts.working: Points may include: tawhid; angels are servants not independent powers; avoid pride after success; lesson of Hunayn (relying on numbers); gratitude. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the ways in which the Qur'an says angels support and protect believers.
parts.answer: Angels guard each person by God's command (13.11); the angels who bear the Throne pray for forgiveness for the believers (40.7); they descend on those who are steadfast, telling them not to fear or grieve (41.30); they bring peace at death to the righteous.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: guardian angels in front and behind (13.11); bearers of the Throne ask forgiveness for believers (40.7); angels descend on the steadfast with good news of Paradise (41.30–31); they greet believers at the gates of Paradise with peace (13.23–24); they take the souls of the good gently; they descend on the Night of Power (97.4); angels send blessings on believers (33.43).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this belief could help a Muslim who feels alone, for example a student studying far from home.
parts.answer: Knowing that angels are with them, protecting them and praying for them, gives comfort, courage and a reminder to behave well.
parts.working: Points may include: not truly alone; comfort in hardship; encourages prayer and remembrance where angels gather; awareness of being recorded encourages good conduct. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the differences between Iblis (Satan) and the angels.
parts.answer: Iblis is of the jinn, created from fire, with free will; angels are created from light and cannot disobey; Iblis refused to prostrate out of pride and became the enemy of humans, while angels obeyed and serve God.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: Iblis was of the jinn (18.50); created from smokeless fire, angels from light; jinn have free will, angels do not; he disobeyed the command to prostrate (2.34); motive of arrogance and envy; expelled and given respite until the Day of Judgement; vowed to mislead humans (7.16–17); angels record deeds and protect, Satan whispers evil; Satan has no power over sincere servants (15.42).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a Muslim can resist the whispering of Satan in daily life.
parts.answer: By remembering God, seeking refuge in Him (e.g. Sura 114), praying regularly, keeping good company and avoiding situations of temptation.
parts.working: Points may include: seeking refuge (Suras 113, 114); dhikr and Qur'an; regular salat; good friends; controlling anger and gaze; awareness that Satan is a clear enemy (35.6). 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the role of the angel Jibril in the life of the Prophet (pbuh).
parts.answer: Jibril brought the first revelation in the cave of Hira and continued to bring the Qur'an over about twenty-three years; he accompanied the Prophet (pbuh) on the Night Journey and Ascension; he taught him how to perform the prayers; he came in human form to ask about Islam, faith and excellence, teaching the Companions; he reviewed the Qur'an with the Prophet (pbuh) every Ramadan, twice in the final year; he supported him at difficult times, such as at Ta'if with the angel of the mountains.
parts.working: Indicative content: First revelation at Hira; brought the Qur'an over about 23 years; Night Journey and Ascension; taught the timings and method of prayer; the Hadith of Jibril (Islam, iman, ihsan); appeared in human form; reviewed the Qur'an each Ramadan; twice in the last year; support at Ta'if; called the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus) in the Qur'an. parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Jibril's role is important for Muslim belief in the Qur'an.
parts.answer: Because the Qur'an came through a trustworthy angel directly from God, Muslims believe it is God's word and not the Prophet's (pbuh) own composition.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Point, development (e.g. revision with Jibril ensured accuracy). parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the differences between angels, jinn and human beings in Islamic belief.
parts.answer: Angels are made from light, have no free will and always obey God; jinn are made from smokeless fire, are unseen, have free will and can be believers or disbelievers — Iblis was one of the jinn; humans are made from clay, have free will and are given the role of vicegerent; jinn and humans will be judged on their choices, while angels are not tested in the same way.
parts.working: Indicative content: Angels — light; no free will; always obey. Jinn — smokeless fire; free will; can be good or bad; Iblis was a jinn. Humans — clay / earth; free will; vicegerents (khalifa); humans and jinn judged on the Last Day. Marked by levels out of 10. parts.label: b
parts.text: Why do you think human beings, with free will, can be honoured above angels? Explain.
parts.answer: Because humans choose to obey God despite temptation, while angels obey by nature; choosing goodness freely is a greater achievement, which is why angels bowed to Adam.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Free choice makes obedience meaningful; humans struggle against desires and Shaytan; evidence — angels told to bow to Adam / Adam taught the names. Model answer: Because humans choose to obey God despite temptation, while angels obey by nature; choosing goodness freely is a greater achievement, which is why angels bowed to Adam.
