parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about angels' visits to prophets other than Muhammad (pbuh), such as Ibrahim, Lut and Maryam, as described in the Qur'an.
parts.answer: Angels came to Ibrahim as guests; he offered them a roasted calf, they did not eat, and they gave news of a son, Ishaq, to Sara; they then went to Lut to warn him and destroy his people for their sins, saving Lut and his family except his wife; Jibril appeared to Maryam as a man to announce the birth of 'Isa (Jesus).
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): Ibrahim's guests (11.69–76; 51.24–37): greeted with peace; he hurried to bring a fat roasted calf; they did not eat and he felt afraid; they said they were sent to the people of Lut; news of Ishaq and then Ya'qub; Sara laughed in surprise at her age; Ibrahim pleaded for Lut's people; at Lut's town the angels came in the form of handsome men; the people rushed to them; Lut was distressed; the angels revealed themselves and told him to leave by night; the town was overturned and stones rained; his wife was left behind; Maryam (19.16–21): the spirit appeared to her as a man; she sought refuge; he said he was a messenger from her Lord to give her a pure son; she asked how, as no man had touched her; it is easy for God; Zakariyya also given news of Yahya by angels (3.39). Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What do these stories show about the roles angels can play in carrying out God's will? Evaluate their importance for Muslim belief.
parts.answer: Angels bring good news and warnings, deliver revelation and carry out God's punishment; this shows God's control and the link between the seen and unseen worlds, though angels act only by His command.
parts.working: Points may include: messengers of good news (births) and warnings; agents of justice; appear in human form; strengthen prophets; support belief in revelation; evaluation for full marks. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why belief in angels is one of the Articles of Faith and how it is connected to the other articles.
parts.answer: The Qur'an lists it with belief in God, books, messengers and the Last Day (2.285; 2.177; 4.136); angels bring revelation (link to books and prophets), record deeds and take souls (link to the Hereafter), carry out God's decree (link to qadr) and show God's greatness (link to tawhid).
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): 2.285 and 2.177 list angels among things believers accept; 4.136 rejecting angels is going far astray; the Hadith of Jibril lists faith in God, angels, books, messengers, the Last Day and qadr; Jibril brought the books to messengers; recording angels and the Angel of Death connect to the Hereafter; Munkar and Nakir question in the grave; angels carry out God's commands, linked to qadr; their obedience shows God's sovereignty and protects tawhid since they are servants, not gods; denying angels would mean denying the Qur'an's own account of its revelation. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Belief in angels has little practical effect on a Muslim's life.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: Disagree: awareness of recording angels encourages good behaviour, belief in guardian angels gives comfort, and angels' obedience is a model; but its effects depend on how seriously the belief is held.
parts.working: Points may include: recording angels and accountability; comfort and protection; model of worship; belief in revelation; some may hold belief only in theory; justified conclusion. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some people say that angels are simply symbols of good forces in nature or in the human mind. Explain why Muslims believe angels are real, separate beings.
parts.answer: The Qur'an describes angels as created beings with names, wings, speech and specific tasks; they appeared to prophets in visible form; Jibril was seen by the Prophet (pbuh) and Companions (Hadith of Jibril); they will testify and act on the Day of Judgement.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: named individuals (Jibril, Mika'il, Malik); described with wings (35.1); speak with God and with prophets (2.30–33); took human form (Maryam; Ibrahim's guests); the Prophet (pbuh) saw Jibril in his true form (53.13–14); Companions saw him as a man in the Hadith of Jibril; angels fought at Badr; they will act on the Last Day; denying them contradicts the Qur'an.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether it matters if a Muslim believes angels are real beings rather than symbols.
parts.answer: Yes, since belief in angels as stated in the Qur'an is an article of faith and turning them into symbols undermines belief in revelation itself; but understanding their exact nature is beyond human knowledge.
parts.working: Points may include: article of faith; revelation's reliability; Jibril as real messenger of the Qur'an; limits of human understanding of the unseen; argued conclusion. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the four levels of belief in al-qadr (divine decree) that Muslim scholars commonly identify, and how the Qur'an supports each one.
parts.answer: The four levels are: God's complete knowledge of everything past, present and future; the recording of all things in the Preserved Tablet; God's will, so that nothing happens unless He wills it; and God's creation of all things. Each is supported by Qur'anic verses such as 6.59, 57.22, 81.29 and 54.49, and human beings still have real choice and responsibility.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): knowledge ('ilm): God knows everything before it happens (6.59); recording (kitaba): all is written in the Preserved Tablet (57.22; 85.22); will (mashi'a): nothing happens unless God wills it (81.29); creation (khalq): God creates all things with measure (54.49); the Hadith of Jibril lists qadr as the sixth article of faith; good and bad occur within His decree, yet humans have choice and are responsible (18.29; 76.3); the balance between decree and human responsibility. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a Muslim who commits a sin should not blame God's decree (al-qadr) for it, and what they should do instead.
parts.answer: Because the person chose the act and is responsible for it; blaming decree is the argument the polytheists used (6.148). The right response is sincere repentance (tawba): asking forgiveness and changing behaviour.
parts.working: Points may include: the decree is hidden from humans, so the sinner made the choice; 6.148 rejects the polytheists' argument; humans have choice and responsibility (76.3; 91.7–10); repentance is always open (39.53); stop the sin, make amends and resolve not to repeat it; a reasoned example. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Prophet (pbuh) told a man to tie his camel and then put his trust in God. Explain what this teaches about tawakkul (trust in God).
parts.answer: Tawakkul means taking all reasonable steps and then relying on God for the outcome, not neglecting effort.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: the man thought trusting God meant leaving the camel untied; the Prophet (pbuh) corrected him; effort is required; results are in God's hands; avoids laziness and fatalism; avoids arrogance in relying on one's own effort; the Prophet's (pbuh) own planning for the Hijra and battles; birds go out in the morning to find food (they do not sit in nests).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of how a Muslim farmer in Punjab could practise tawakkul.
parts.answer: Using good seed, irrigation and modern methods while praying for rain and accepting the result; paying zakat on the harvest and not despairing in a bad season.
parts.working: 2 marks for each example: 1 for effort/action, 1 for linking it to trust in God (e.g. du'a, patience, gratitude).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A promising young cricketer from Sialkot is badly injured just before an important tournament. Describe how belief in al-qadr could help him respond.
parts.answer: He would accept that the injury is part of God's decree and a test, be patient without despair, look after his recovery, and trust that God may have something better for him.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: accepting it as God's decree; patience (sabr) rewarded (2.155–157); avoiding blaming others or God; following treatment (taking means); du'a for recovery; something disliked may be good (2.216); hope of reward for illness; gratitude for other blessings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the verse 'perhaps you dislike something which is good for you' (2.216) might change the way a Muslim sees disappointments.
parts.answer: It reminds them that humans see only part of the picture; God knows best, so disappointments may hide benefits, which brings hope and patience.
parts.working: Points may include: limited human knowledge; God's wisdom; examples where failure led to better results; patience and hope; trusting God's plan. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Qur'an says believers will be tested with fear, hunger and loss of wealth, lives and crops, and that those who are patient say 'To God we belong and to Him we return' (2.155–156). Describe what this passage teaches about hardship.
parts.answer: Hardship is part of God's decree and a test for everyone; patience is required; believers accept that everything belongs to God and will return to Him; the patient receive blessings and mercy and are rightly guided (2.157).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: everyone is tested; types of tests listed; good news for the patient; the phrase recognises God's ownership of all things; return to God reminds of the Hereafter; blessings and mercy promised (2.157); hardship is not necessarily punishment; Muslims say this phrase at news of death or loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Muslims say 'To God we belong and to Him we return' when they hear of a death.
parts.answer: It expresses acceptance of God's decree, reminds them that life is a trust which returns to its owner, comforts the bereaved, and recalls their own return to God.
parts.working: Points may include: acceptance; comfort; remembrance of one's own death; ownership by God; following the Qur'an's teaching; patience rewarded. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the meaning of each of these terms: (i) qadr; (ii) tawakkul; (iii) sabr; (iv) shukr.
parts.answer: (i) God's decree/measure of all things; (ii) trust and reliance on God; (iii) patience/steadfastness; (iv) gratitude/thankfulness.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Prophet (pbuh) said that the affair of a believer is wonderful, because in good times he is grateful and in hard times he is patient, and both are good for him. Explain this teaching with reference to al-qadr.
parts.answer: Because everything comes from God's decree, a believer gains reward in every situation: gratitude in ease and patience in hardship, so no circumstance is a loss.
parts.working: Points may include: both ease and hardship decreed; shukr in blessings; sabr in difficulty; reward either way; contentment and balance; examples. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what Muslims mean by belief in al-qadr (divine decree).
parts.answer: God knows everything that has happened and will happen; everything is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz); nothing happens except by God's will; God is the Creator of everything, including human actions; yet humans have been given free will to choose and are responsible for their choices; belief in decree, good and bad, is an Article of Faith.
parts.working: Indicative content: God's complete knowledge of past, present and future; recorded in the Preserved Tablet; everything happens by His will; He creates all things; humans still choose and are accountable; belief in qadr, both good and bad, is part of iman (mentioned in the Hadith of Jibril); decree does not excuse wrongdoing. parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how belief in al-qadr can help a Muslim whose family business has failed.
parts.answer: They can accept the loss patiently as part of God's plan and a test, avoid despair or blaming others, and still make fresh efforts, trusting God for the outcome.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Patience and acceptance — a test from God; hope, since God's plan may contain good not yet seen; continued effort and trust (tie the camel), e.g. restarting with better planning. Model answer: They can accept the loss patiently as part of God's plan and a test, avoid despair or blaming others, and still make fresh efforts, trusting God for the outcome. parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the Qur'an shows that human beings have free will and are responsible for their actions, even though God has decreed all things.
parts.answer: The Qur'an says humans are shown the way and may be grateful or ungrateful (76.3), let whoever wills believe or disbelieve (18.29), no compulsion in religion (2.256), each soul earns what it does (74.38), and life and death are created to test who is best in deeds (67.2); a test requires choice; God's knowledge does not force a person's choice.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): 76.3 guided to the way, grateful or ungrateful; 18.29 whoever wills let him believe; 2.256 no compulsion; 91.7–10 the soul inspired with right and wrong, successful one purifies it; 74.38 every soul held for what it earned; 67.2 test; 53.39 nothing for a person except what he strives for; prophets sent to call people to choose; reward and punishment would be unjust without choice; God's knowledge is like knowing the outcome without forcing it; God's will includes giving humans choice. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the idea of life as a test only makes sense if humans have real choice.
parts.answer: A test where the result is forced would be meaningless and unjust; reward and punishment depend on free choice.
parts.working: Points may include: 67.2 test of deeds; examination analogy; justice of God; responsibility; accountability on the Day of Judgement. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Floods in Pakistan in recent years have destroyed many homes and crops. Explain how belief in al-qadr can help families affected by such disasters and also motivate others to help.
parts.answer: Victims can find patience and hope by seeing the disaster as a test from God with reward for patience; others see it as a test of their generosity and a duty to help; belief in qadr does not mean doing nothing, so preparation and relief efforts are required.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: disasters as tests (2.155); 'to God we belong and to Him we return' (2.156) brings comfort; reward for those who are patient; those who die in disasters can be counted as martyrs in some Hadiths; communities tested by how they respond; helping victims is a duty (zakat, sadaqa); preparation and better building is taking the means; avoid blaming the victims.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Belief in God's decree means people should not try to prevent disasters.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: Disagree: Islam teaches taking the means (tying the camel), so building flood defences, planning and protecting the environment are required; accepting decree applies after effort.
parts.working: Points may include: tawakkul with effort; 'Umar and the plague; khilafa duties; some disasters linked to human actions (30.41); balanced conclusion. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the story of Qarun (Korah) in the Qur'an and what it teaches about success and decree.
parts.answer: Qarun, from Musa's people, was given huge treasures; he became arrogant and claimed his wealth came from his own knowledge (28.78); he ignored advice to be humble and generous; the earth swallowed him and his house; those who envied him realised that provision is given or withheld by God.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: very rich, keys of his treasures were heavy for strong men; told not to exult and to seek the Hereafter while not forgetting his share of the world (28.76–77); he said he received it because of his knowledge; showed off his wealth; some people wished they had the same; the earth swallowed him (28.81); those who envied him thanked God they were not like him; success is from God.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how belief in al-qadr should affect a successful businessperson's attitude to their wealth.
parts.answer: They should see success as a gift and test from God, be grateful and humble, pay zakat and help others, rather than taking all the credit.
parts.working: Points may include: gratitude (14.7); humility; wealth as amana; zakat and charity; contrast with Qarun; fair treatment of workers. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When plague broke out in Syria, the caliph 'Umar decided not to enter the area. When asked whether he was running away from God's decree, he said he was moving from God's decree to God's decree. Explain what he meant.
parts.answer: Taking precautions is itself within God's decree; choosing the safer path does not deny decree but uses the means God has given; this was supported by the Prophet's (pbuh) teaching about not entering or leaving a plague area.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: both outcomes are within God's decree; humans must choose the wise option; avoiding danger is permitted and required; 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf reported the Prophet's (pbuh) instruction about plague; 'Umar gave the example of a valley with fertile and barren sides; precaution is part of tawakkul; consultation with Companions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this example applies to Muslims during a modern epidemic.
parts.answer: Following medical advice, vaccinations, quarantine and hygiene is part of trusting God, not against it.
parts.working: Points may include: health precautions; quarantine as in the Hadith; vaccines and treatment; du'a with precautions; protecting others; avoiding fatalism. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 'If God has decreed everything, humans cannot be responsible for what they do.' Explain how Muslims answer this argument.
parts.answer: God's knowledge of what people will choose does not force them to choose it; humans are given intellect, guidance and free will, and they experience making real choices; God's justice requires accountability only for what people chose; people are not held responsible for what is outside their control; therefore decree and responsibility exist together, and the decree cannot be used as an excuse for sin.

parts.text: Explain how belief in al-qadr should affect a Muslim's attitude to both success and hardship.
parts.answer: In success they should be grateful and humble, knowing it came by God's will; in hardship they should be patient and avoid despair, knowing it is a test and that God's plan is wise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 'If God has already decreed everything, there is no point in making du'a (personal prayer).' Explain how Muslims answer this objection.
parts.answer: Du'a itself is part of God's decree and a means He has set for outcomes; God commands people to call on Him (40.60) and promises to answer; du'a is worship and builds the relationship with God; answers may come as the request, protection from harm or reward in the Hereafter.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: God commands du'a and promises a response (40.60; 2.186); du'a is worship in itself; causes and means are part of qadr (like medicine); God knows what we will ask and has written the response; answers come in different forms (granted, harm averted, reward saved); the Prophet (pbuh) made du'a constantly, e.g. at Badr; changes the person making it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the view that du'a mainly changes the person praying rather than the outcome.
parts.answer: Du'a certainly changes the person (humility, hope, patience), but Muslims also believe God truly responds and changes outcomes within His decree; both aspects matter.
parts.working: Points may include: psychological benefits; real belief in God's response; examples from the Qur'an (Zakariyya, Ayyub); the Prophet's (pbuh) du'a; justified conclusion. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'If God has decreed that I will pass, I will pass whether I study or not.' Explain why this view is a misunderstanding of al-qadr.
parts.answer: God's decree includes the means as well as the result; humans do not know what is decreed and must act on what they are commanded; the Prophet (pbuh) told his Companions to act, as each will be eased towards what he was created for; God's knowledge does not force choice; laziness is a choice for which one is accountable.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): decree is unknown to us, so we cannot use it as an excuse; the Companions asked whether to rely on what was written and the Prophet (pbuh) said 'act, for each will be eased' (well-known Hadith); outcomes come through causes; 53.39 nothing for a person except what he strives for; tie the camel; the Prophet (pbuh) planned the Hijra and battles; 'Umar's reply at the plague; God's knowledge is not compulsion; using qadr to excuse sin was the argument of the polytheists (6.148); responsibility on the Day of Judgement. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How should belief in al-qadr affect the same student's feelings after receiving the exam results, whether good or bad? Explain.
parts.answer: If successful, gratitude and humility, recognising God's help; if not, patience without despair, learning lessons and trying again, trusting God's wisdom.
parts.working: Points may include: gratitude vs pride; patience vs despair (57.23 'so that you do not despair over what has passed you, nor exult over what He has given you'); review effort; trust God's plan; future planning. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Muslims understand the existence of suffering and evil in a world decreed by a good and merciful God.
parts.answer: Suffering tests faith and patience (2.155; 67.2); it purifies sins; it reveals strength and compassion in others; much evil results from human free choice (30.41); this life is not the final place of justice; God's wisdom is beyond human understanding (2.216; the story of Musa and al-Khidr, 18.65–82); reward in the Hereafter outweighs suffering.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): life as a test; hardship removes sins (Hadith that even a thorn's prick expiates sins); free will causes much evil, e.g. war, injustice; corruption appears because of what people's hands have earned (30.41); suffering brings out patience, charity and compassion; Musa and al-Khidr: apparent evils had hidden wisdom (18.65–82); limited human knowledge (2.216); God is just and all will be put right on the Day of Judgement; suffering of prophets (Ayyub) shows it is not a sign of God's anger; mercy shown in relief and reward. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The story of Musa and al-Khidr is the best answer to the problem of suffering.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: It powerfully shows that apparent harms can hide wisdom, but on its own it may not satisfy those suffering now; it works best with belief in the Hereafter and human responsibility.
parts.working: Points may include: story's lesson about hidden wisdom; limits for victims of injustice; combine with free will and Hereafter; personal experience; justified judgement. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the life of the Prophet (pbuh) shows a balance between careful effort and trust in God's decree.
parts.answer: He planned the Hijra carefully (secret timing, Thawr, guide, food, covering tracks) yet trusted God in the cave (9.40); at Badr he arranged the lines and then prayed intensely; at the Trench he dug defences; he used medicine and taught that every disease has a cure; he accepted losses such as his sons' deaths and Uhud with patience.
parts.working: Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point): Hijra planning and 9.40 'God is with us'; Badr: choosing the wells, arranging ranks, then long du'a; Uhud: placing archers, then accepting the setback; Trench: digging; Hudaybiyya: accepting terms that seemed unfavourable but trusting God; encouragement of medical treatment; tie your camel; patience at the death of his son Ibrahim, saying the eyes weep and the heart grieves but we say only what pleases our Lord; Ta'if: effort, rejection and du'a; never fatalistic, never relying only on himself. Levels: 9–10 a detailed, accurate and well-organised account using most of these points with names and events; 6–8 a good account with some detail; 3–5 a basic outline with gaps or some inaccuracy; 1–2 a few relevant facts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Most people today rely too much on their own plans and too little on God.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: There is truth in it, as modern life emphasises control and self-reliance and anxiety is high; but some also neglect effort in the name of trust; a balanced Muslim view combines both.
parts.working: Points may include: modern self-reliance and anxiety; neglect of du'a; opposite error of fatalism; examples; the Prophet's (pbuh) balance; justified conclusion. 4 marks: a well-developed, reasoned answer with a relevant example; 3: good reasoning, partly developed; 2: some relevant reasoning; 1: a simple statement.
